WINNING OF CANADIAN CHAMPIONSHIP BY NOVA SCOTIA RINK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure all hon. members from Nova Scotia will tender their sympathy to my deskmate, the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher), to the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) and to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), as well as to all other ardent curlers in the house, on the fact that teams representing those various places in the Canadian championship bowed to the Nova Scotia team in Halifax on Saturday last.
I am sure, sir, that all of them will join with us from Nova Scotia in tendering our congratulations to the Kentville rink consisting of Wallace Knock, Fred Dyke, George Hansen and Donald Oyler, a very youthful and, from the national standpoint, inexperienced team. They not only won the dominion championship, but won it in such a way that their record can never be broken, and probably will never be equalled.

subtopic: WINNING OF CANADIAN CHAMPIONSHIP BY NOVA SCOTIA RINK
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I say how pleased and happy the city of Halifax and the province of Nova Scotia were to entertain those who participated in the Dominion curling championship. Mr. Speaker, I should

There have never been any joint ministers in the departments in the periods referred to in the questions. The only department which had an associate minister was the Department of National Defence, and his functions are a matter of public record, as they appear in the Department of National Defence Act of 1940.
Acting ministers are appointed from time to time to act in the absence of the ministers. The names and duration of periods of office of the acting ministers of justice and finance for the dates referred to are as follows: Department of Justice-April 3, 1936, Hon P J A Cardin; November 11, 1941, Hon. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Caldwell) knows that the government of the United Kingdom has been approached to see whether they have any objection to the publication of documents related to the discussions referred to in this motion. Of course hon. members realize that it is not usual to publish documents connected with negotiations between governments, but only to publish the agreed conclusions. Nevertheless we have asked the views of the United Kingdom government about this motion.
As a controversy has arisen in debate respecting the position taken by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) at London in May of 1950, and by the government since that time, I feel I should make the position clear at once.
The United Kingdom authorities took the position in May of 1950 "that all obligations under the 'have regard to' clause might be considered to have been taken care of." The Minister of Trade and Commerce said that this was a matter which could only be settled by the Canadian cabinet on his return to Ottawa. After discussion with his colleagues, the Minister of Trade and Commerce advised the chancellor of the exchequer of the United Kingdom that the Canadian government was in accord with the conclusions in the agreed record of the meeting held with the United Kingdom authorities while he was in London. That is one of

Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime
Minister): May I give an answer to a question submitted on March 6 by the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Jones)? The question was:
Did the government of British Columbia make representations in regard to the fruit growers, and if so, did they receive that answer?
That was in reference to the answer that had been given just before the hon. member had put his question. I told him I would have to look at the correspondence; that I knew members of the British Columbia legislature were concerned but I did not want to

make a positive statement about the government of British Columbia without looking at the correspondence. I am now given the following answer.
The government of British Columbia did make representations in regard to the fruit growers who suffered losses in the winter of 1949-50. We considered the matter and came to the conclusion that as the loss was not beyond the capacity of the provincial government to handle, and as there was no precedent for the provision of federal assistance in similar cases, assistance could not be provided by the federal government for the rehabilitation of damaged orchards; and the government of British Columbia was so informed.

speakeroldname: Hon. Douglas Abbott (Minister of Finance) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to present a measure to provide for the continuance in force of the Foreign Exchange Control Act until sixty days after the commencement of the first session of parliament commencing in the year 1953.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this resolution seeks leave to introduce a bill providing for the extension of the Foreign Exchange Control Act for a further two-year period. The original measure, enacted by parliament in 1947, provided that the act should lapse sixty days after the commencement of the first session of parliament in 1949. On March 17, 1949, I introduced a resolution, which was subsequently embodied in legislation approved by parliament, providing for the continuance in force of the act until sixty days after the commencement of the first session of parliament in 1951. The effect of the present bill, when it is enacted, will be to postpone the termination date for a period expiring sixty days after the commencement of the first session of parliament in 1953.
When I introduced a similar resolution two years ago, I described the Foreign Exchange Control Act as a measure of national defence. The developments of the past two years, and particularly of the past six months, have, I think, illustrated the correctness of this description, as well, of course, as the continued need for the measure itself. It is because the government believes that this measure of national defence continues to be necessary that we are asking the house to agree to retain it for another two years. We all wish that the state of the world were such that there were no longer any need to retain the powers provided in this act. It is no affection for controls as

such which moves us to seek a prolongation. On the contrary, as I shall show the house in some detail, we have progressively reduced the extent of the control which is in fact exercised under the act, and we hope to continue in this direction as long as we are able. When, however, we are confronted with the question, as we are at this time, whether we are prepared to abandon the machinery itself by allowing the act to expire, then we feel that only one answer is possible.
There is no need for me, after the discussion which has already taken place in the house since the commencement of this session, to elaborate on the unsettled state of the world. Nor is there, I believe, any need to introduce any elaborate arguments to establish that one aspect, and a very important one, of our economic preparedness must be the control over our foreign exchange resources. I am not able to relate in detail to the house, because I do not know, what foreign exchange pressures we may be under as we and our allies step up the pace of our military preparedness. But I feel that members on all sides of the house will agree that we shall be better able to cope with the pressures that do arise if we retain this instrument of control than if we abandon it.
Even without the pressures of war and near war, the foreign exchange situation of Canada tends to be an extremely variable one. This is illustrated in the wide swings to which our foreign exchange reserves have been subjected since the end of the war. In this connection may I express my personal regret that the 1950 report of the foreign exchange control board, which will include the detailed relevant statistics for the last calendar year, is not yet available. I had hoped that it would be ready in time for this debate, but I am now advised that it will be another three or four weeks before some of the figures can toe finalized and the report printed and tabled. Some of the figures which I shall use in this statement therefore will necessarily be very preliminary and tentative. However, hon. members are already aware from published reports that our official reserves in gold and U.S. dollars, which amounted to approximately $1,500 million at the end of 1945, fell during 1946 by approximately $250 million and in 1947 by nearly $750 million. In 1948, on the other hand, they rose by nearly $500 million, in 1949 by $120 million and in 1950 by $625 million. These are very formidable changes from year to year and they illustrate better than words the size of the external pressures to which our economy is subject. These

pressures arise partly as a result of the importance of external transactions in our economy-

speechtext:
Yes. I believe the last
quarterly figures have been published. Our reserves at the end of September-I am speaking from memory now-were approximately $1,800 million U.S. dollars, and they were about the same at the end of the year. Those figures were available early in January.
As I was saying, these pressures arise partly as a result of the importance of external transactions in our economy, partly as a result of the nature of our trading relationships with the two economic areas of major importance to us, the United States and the sterling area; partly as a result of our proximity to the United States and the large volume of U.S. capital investment in Canada. Whatever the causes may be, it is the case that throughout the post-war period our foreign exchange situation has shown itself to be capable of very rapid change from year to year. The existence of exchange control has been helpful in coping with these changes and in moderating their effects, though it cannot, of course, be claimed that this control by itself provides any guarantee of stability. It is essentially a defensive instrument.
It may be of value to the house if I review now the highlights of our foreign exchange experience during the past two years,-that is, since the act was last extended.
I must begin by recalling the foreign exchange difficulties which arose in 1947 and which resulted in the loss, by the end of that year, of nearly two-thirds of the reserves with which we emerged from the war. In tackling these difficulties we were obliged temporarily to do a number of unpleasant and unpopular things, such as restrict imports and ration pleasure travel involving U.S. dollar outlays. We substantially reduced the rate of our own foreign lending and we borrowed some capital in the United States. However, we placed the greatest emphasis on a positive approach. We sought to achieve a closer approach to equilibrium in our bilateral balance of payments with the United States and the sterling area by developing our exports to the United States and by encouraging imports into Canada from the United Kingdom and other parts of the sterling area.
12, 1951
Foreign Exchange Control Act
This program, which was supported by the general fiscal and economic policies of the government, was successful in improving our balance of payments and stemming the loss of reserves. In the course of 1948, as I have noted, we added nearly $500 million to our official holdings, of which $150 million was borrowed. Our over-all balance of payments in that year showed a current account surplus of over $450 million; our current account deficit with the United States alone was reduced from over $1,100 million to less than $400 million.
In 1949 we continued to add to our reserves, though at the more moderate rate of $120 million. Our over-all current account surplus was reduced to $180 million, the change as compared with the previous year occurring mainly in our transactions with the United States, and reflecting mainly increased imports into Canada and increased travel expenditures and dividend payments involving U.S. dollar outlays.
The most significant development in the foreign exchange field in 1949 was of course the change in the international exchange rate structure which was inaugurated by the thirty per cent devaluation of sterling in September of that year. This action by the United Kingdom was followed by similar action by all other sterling area countries with the exception of Pakistan; and most western European countries immediately depreciated their exchange rate to the same or a lesser degree. As a result of these changes a new and very drastic exchange rate structure emerged and a completely new situation was created for the Canadian dollar. In appraising the new situation the government came to the conclusion that the Canadian interest would best be served by reducing the value of the Canadian dollar in terms of U.S. dollars by approximately nine per cent. We felt, in the face of the very large depreciation in the value of sterling and most other currencies, that some change must be made in the value of the Canadian dollar. Our competitive position at home and abroad was strong, but we did not feel that Canadian producers should be subjected to the full strain of a thirty per cent reduction in the exchange value of the currencies of some of our principal competitors in the home and foreign markets. On the other hand, the devaluation of sterling and other currencies represented, in part, an effort on the part of the countries concerned to use the price system to redress the great unbalance that still persisted in their trade with the dollar countries. This effort would have been nullified, so far as Canada was concerned, had we not allowed some appreciation of the Canadian dollar in relation to these currencies. Out of

Foreign Exchange Control Act these conflicting considerations we reached the decision of September 1949 to reduce the exchange value of the Canadian dollar by about nine per cent, which involved an appreciation of our currency in relation to sterling of approximately twenty-five per cent.
In the latter part of 1949, and in the course of 1950, important new factors emerged affecting in an important way our foreign exchange position. One of these was a very sharp drop in our exports to the United Kingdom and other sterling area countries. Members of the house will recall that at the commonwealth ministers of finance meeting which took place in London in July, 1949, to consider the problem raised by the very sharp decline in the sterling area's gold and dollar reserves, the sterling area countries agreed to reduce their dollar drawings on the sterling area dollar pool in respect of dollar imports by an amount equivalent to twenty-five per cent of 1948 imports. It is, of course, impossible to say to what extent the decline in sterling area purchases in Canada which occurred in 1950 was due to the tightening of import restrictions consequent upon this decision, to what extent it was due to normal economic forces set in train by the exchange devaluations of September 1949, and to what extent it was due to the continued recovery of production in the non-dollar world and consequent availability of supplies on economic terms for payment other than in dollars. Whatever may have been the factors operating, our exports to the United Kingdom fell from $710 million in 1949 to $470 million in 1950, and our exports to the rest of the sterling area from $300 million in 1949 to $200 million in 1950-an aggregate decline of over $300 million, or thirty per cent, in our exports to the sterling area in one year. Before the war, nearly half our exports went to the sterling area; by 1949 this had been reduced to a third; and in 1950 the proportion going there was substantially less than one quarter.
On the other hand, in recent years, the total value of our imports from these countries has increased very considerably, percentagewise, though even now the sterling area supplies us with only slightly more than twenty per cent of our total imports compared with nearly thirty per cent before the war. The United Kingdom, which had already succeeded in increasing its exports to Canada from less than $150 million in 1946 to $300 million in 1949, increased them still further to just over $400 million in 1950. Other sterling area countries increased their exports to us from $190 million in 1949 to $240 million in 1950. This increase in imports from the sterling area, helping as it has done to redress the


balance of payments between this part of the world and Canada, has been a most welcome development, and I should like to express the satisfaction of the government at the success which has attended British efforts in this direction. The development of exports to Canada is the course of action which I strongly urged on my colleagues, the ministers of finance of the sterling area countries, at the commonwealth gathering of ministers of finance in July 1949, to which I referred a moment ago. We in Canada believe-and I am sure that all members of the house will agree-that it is in the interests of all concerned that any necessary correction of the unbalance in accounts between Canada and the sterling area should be achieved through an expansion in our imports rather than through a contraction in our exports.
Primarily as a result of the developments I have mentioned affecting our import and export trade with the sterling area, our current account surplus with this part of the world, which was $578 million in 1949, virtually disappeared in 1950 according to the preliminary estimates. After taking all capital items-including our extensions of credit- into consideration, the sterling area made net payments, mainly in U.S. dollars, of nearly $500 million to Canada in 1949. In 1950, on the other hand, the balance has so far been redressed that there was in the year apparently only a very small net transfer of gold and U.S. dollars between Canada and the countries of the sterling area.
The improvement in the sterling area's balance of payments with Canada is, of course, only one aspect of the very remarkable and welcomed improvement which has occurred in the over-all dollar position of that area since the devaluation of sterling. This improvement is reflected in the gold and dollar reserves of the United Kingdom which have risen from $1,425 million at the end of September 1949-and an even lower figure immediately before devaluation-to $3,300 million at the end of 1950. Some part of this increase is of course attributable to ECA and other external assistance, but during the past year the sterling area as a whole has been earning a substantial surplus in its dollar transactions.
In the light of this improved position, it is the earnest hope of the Canadian government that the governments of the United Kingdom and other sterling area countries will give earnest consideration to the possibility of relaxing the present severe import restrictions, particularly those of a discriminatory character, on imports from Canada. We recognize of course that there are a number of uncertainties and unfavourable elements in

the British situation which justify a certain degree of caution. The dollar surplus, particularly that which has occurred since Korea, has been achieved in part by a very sharp increase in the prices of the primary products exported from sterling area countries other than the United Kingdom. The United Kingdom has had to give up a much larger volume of exports to obtain the same volume of imports from other sterling area countries, and this has absorbed a large part of the increase in output of the United Kingdom during the past year. Even so, the balances held in London by other sterling area countries-the counterpart, in some measure, of their surplus dollar earnings transferred to the United Kingdom-have risen very substantially, and they constitute a claim on British productive capacity. Moreover, the rearmament effort of the United Kingdom will absorb an increasing share of British resources, and particularly perhaps in those fields in which the dollar export drive has been most successful.
For these reasons we can appreciate why the British chancellor of the exchequer has pointed to the necessity of some degree of caution in appraising the outlook for the dollar position of the United Kingdom. At the same time we feel justified, for our part, in expressing the strong hope that the caution will not be excessive. Some of the sterling area countries have already taken steps to reduce their restrictions on dollar imports, and it is to be hoped that others, including the United Kingdom, will take advantage of their present opportunities to do likewise. In the present circumstances we urge this course not so much because of any desire to widen the markets for Canadian products-which, with very few exceptions, are finding a ready enough sale at the present time-but rather on account of our desire to see competitive conditions re-established over as wide an area of trade as possible and concrete evidence given of the determination of all our trading partners to move as rapidly as they can towards the achievement of those principles of non-discrimination and liberalism which are the declared policy of the government in international trade.
1 revert now to the main developments in our foreign exchange position during the past two years. The first, as I have pointed out, has been the virtual elimination of the surplus in our balance of payments with the sterling area. Our exports to western European countries have also been substantially reduced-by about one-third- while our imports have increased somewhat, though they remain disappointingly small. In consequence our current account surplus
Foreign Exchange Control Act with that part of the world is substantially less than it was a few years ago.
In some ways the most striking development in our exchange position during the past few years has been the great expansion in our exports to the United States. Those rose from $1,000 million in 1947 to $1,500 million in 1949 and to over $2,000 million in 1950. The high level of economic activity prevailing in the United States, combined with the enterprise of Canadians in producing the right goods at the right prices and taking advantage of their opportunities and seeking out new markets, plus the more favourable conditions of entry for certain important products arranged in tariff negotiations with the United States-these were among the factors responsible for this remarkable increase in our exports to the United States. It had been our hope, when we got into exchange difficulties in 1947, that once the emergency, which required us to impose restrictive measures on imports and travel, had been overcome, we would be able to achieve the necessary correction in our position through an expansion of exports. These hopes have, as the house is aware, been realized, and, in line with the policy announced at the time the restrictions were first imposed, they have been progressively reduced as our exchange position has improved. At the beginning of this year the last of the import restrictions imposed' under the Emergency Exchange Conservation Act was eliminated, and that act itself has in consequence lapsed. So far as travel is concerned, we are again in the happy position where Canadians can obtain U.S. funds to cover all travel requirements without being subject to any ration.	.
The current account deficit in our transactions with the United States was reduced from the very large figure of $1,100 million in 1947 to an amount of the order of $400 million in 1950. It will be apparent from what I have said that this improvement is mainly due to the increase in our exports; the value of our imports was not substantially different, though rising rather rapidly in the latter months of 1950. Increased gold production also played its part in reducing our current deficit with the United States. On the other hand, interest and dividend payments have risen very markedly in recent years.
The reduction in the current account deficit with the United States in recent years, though very substantial, has fallen short of the reduction in our surplus with the sterling area and other countries. In consequence, our over-all current account surplus, which reached the very high figure of $450 million in 1948, was reduced to $180 million in 1949 and gave way to a deficit of the order of $300 million in 1950.

Foreign Exchange Control Act
The developments in our current account position ill 1950, though important, were overshadowed by those relating to capital transactions. In each year since the end of the war, quite substantial sums of capital have come to this country from abroad, particularly from the United States, for direct investment in Canadian industry and to participate in the development of our natural resources. The consequence and the counterpart of this capital inflow has, of course, been a deepening of our economic structure and a growth in our output and our economic capacity which enables us to assume the additional foreign exchange charges resulting from the capital inflow. In the course of 1950, and particularly after the outbreak of hostilities in Korea, a massive inflow of capital of quite a different type developed. This consisted in the purchase by United States investors of marketable Canadian securities, particularly government of Canada obligations. The scale of the capital inflow is reflected in the increase of nearly $600 million in our reserves of gold and U.S. dollars which occurred between June 30 and September 30.
The ardent desire on the part of United States investors to increase their holdings of Canadian securities, and particularly government of Canada securities, was of course flattering to Canada. However, like most flattery, it had its serious drawbacks. In the first place, the bulk of the capital inflow was not for the purpose of helping directly in the development of our economic resources. It was based rather on a favourable general attitude towards our economic future, and in particular on an anticipation that the Canadian exchange rate would be resorted to parity with the United States dollar. In consequence this capital had elements of volatility and speculativeness which is not associated with the direct investment of capital. Moreover, it was an expensive proceeding involving the incurring of additional foreign indebtedness which was not balanced by a corresponding increase in our economic capacity but merely by an increase in our liquid balances of gold and U.S. dollars. Furthermore the very large inflows of exchange inevitably increased the liquid resources available for investment in Canada, and the direct and indirect demand for securities resulting from the capital inflow tended to create very easy money conditions at a time when the growing pressures on our material resources made it desirable that our monetary and credit, as well as our fiscal policies, should be of an anti-inflationary character.
In the statement which I made on September 30, I outlined in some detail the


reasons why the government found it impossible to go on buying all the funds being offered by United States investors at a premium of ten per cent, and the reasons why we felt it unwise, in the circumstances prevailing, to fix a new exchange rate for the Canadian dollar at parity with the United States dollar or any other definite level. I do not think it necessary to go over that ground again. After consulting with the international monetary fund, the government announced its decision to suspend official quotations for the Canadian dollar and allow the exchange rate to be determined by the forces of supply and demand in the market.
The general structure of exchange control has, of course, been retained under the new conditions, although the process' of relaxation which has been in progress during the past couple of years has been accelerated since last October. In the public announcement I made on September 30 last I explained the main changes we were making consequential on the decision to free the exchange rate- the abolition of the so-called unofficial market for Canadian dollars, the withdrawal of restrictions on the types of forward exchange contracts residents may enter into with Canadian banks, and the replacement of the previous requirement that residents coming into possession of foreign exchange must sell it forthwith by one authorizing them to merely declare it forthwith and choose their own time for selling it within a three months' period.
Another change recently made makes it possible for Canadians selling services in the U.S. dollar area to accept Canadian as well as U.S. funds in payment. A further change eases the conditions under which currently earned profits may be remitted to the United States without awaiting the completion of a fiscal year. Canadians going to take up residence in the U.S. dollar area have had their annual allotment of transferable funds increased from a maximum of $12,500 to one of $25,000, and after a three-year period are now permitted to deal with any remainder of their Canadian assets in the same way as other non-residents.
I have already referred to the withdrawal in October of the previous restrictions on pleasure travel in the United States dollar area. The exemption from any form H permit requirement, previously $25 of which $10 could be in United States funds, was increased in October to $100 of which $50 could be in United States funds. We have this month further amended this provision so that the entire $100 can be in United States dollars. At the same time the amount of United

States currency which residents are authorized to hold has been progressively raised to the present level of $100, and the general exemption from the use of permit has also been increased to $100. As a consequence of these changes a great many Canadians having occasion to make relatively small remittances in United States funds or to take relatively short trips to the United States are able to do so without any formalities resulting from the existence of foreign exchange control.
Last week the regulations governing securities transactions were broadened and simplified by removing the distinction between Canadian government domestic securities and corporation securities in connection with exchanges of securities in Canada by nonresidents and in the United States by residents.
In fact, when one considers the very substantial relaxations in foreign exchange policies and procedures regarding United States dollar transactions effected during the past couple of years, and when one bears in mind the fact that virtually no restrictions have at any time been placed on exchange transactions with the sterling area, one feels entitled to regard the exchange control as substantially a stand-by instrument. At the present time we have no restrictions on current account transactions, and the board approves the great majority of the applications it receives involving capital payment. It is the hope and expectation of the government that it will be possible to continue these liberal arrangements; and our purpose is to continue along this path of relaxation and simplification. But, as I have already intimated to the house, we believe that there are too many uncertainties in the present world situation to warrant the abandonment of this defensive instrument. We have had too much experience of the rapidity with which our situation, and, what may be equally important, attitudes towards our situation can change to warrant us in projecting the present favourable position into the difficult years that lie immediately ahead.
We cannot take the risk of leaving ourselves without an instrument of control which we can again bring into use if external factors threaten to add seriously to the difficulties which we shall have in any case to face.
It is for these reasons that the government asks the house to approve this measure extending the Foreign Exchange Control Act for a further two-year period. At the end of that time parliament will again have an opportunity of deciding whether in the
Foreign Exchange Control Act circumstances then prevailing, the public interest still requires the continuance of exchange control.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few observations on the interesting statement we have heard; it contained a great many figures of trade and other matters, but these of course I will not attempt to go into in detail at this time.
I was struck by one or two remarks the minister made, particularly toward the end of his statement. He spoke of the board in the future as being substantially something in the nature of a stand-by organization. On the other hand, as I understand it, he asks that it be continued with all the powers, far-reaching as they are, which at present exist.
I was sorry the minister had not made clearer-although one might hardly have expected him to do so-the reason for the great change of heart that took place last year. That is very important, when one considers the conclusion to which the minister finally came, one which had been pressed upon him for many months previously. I shall read from his statement of last September, when he said:
It has been decided not to establish any new fixed parity for the Canadian dollar at this time, nor to prescribe any new official fixed rates on exchange.
Then he added this, which I greatly welcomed, and which I think everyone welcomed:
Instead rates of exchange will be determined by conditions of supply and demand for foreign currencies in Canada.
Some of us had been trying to persuade the minister for many months that the time had come to take that action, and of course we were glad when it finally came. I should like just to encourage the minister-and I am sure even ministers like to have encouragement-by quoting to him words which I am sure will be familiar to him:
Joy shall be in heaven over one sinner that repen-teth, more than over ninety and nine just persons, which need no repentance.
I hope the minister will take that quotation in the spirit in which it is given.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: But he is not a sinner.

speechtext:
I wish to review briefly the course of the measure we are now asked to renew, as I understand it, without change. We remember this, that in 1946-the minister said 1947, but I think it was a slip on his part-we in this party, while we agreed that some measure of control was then necessary, asked for less rigidity. We

Foreign Exchange Control Act asked that there should be some measure of flexibility introduced into the act. However, that was not considered possible.
I wish to say a word or two about the results which have ensued. As we look back -and this has never been admitted by the government; the minister was far from admitting it today-I think it is perfectly clear that, for a very long time past-I am not saying as far back as the end of the war, because there were peculiar circumstances at that time-there just has not been enough wisdom in the wisest and best experts in finance in the world to determine what is a proper rate of exchange. I do not blame them for not being able to determine what is a proper rate. What I do blame them for is trying to determine a rate at all.
Let me recall to the minds of hon. members what happened in 1947, when it was perfectly clear that the 1946 restoration of the dollar to parity had been an overvaluation. At that time we will all remember-and the minister told us-that we lost altogether about a billion in American exchange, so that in 1947 we had to have these measures. I have referred to them as legislation by radio, but the minister has always disagreed with that, so we will just leave it as a disagreement. That was the time when he became associated with the word "austerity," because a great many measures had to be introduced then, by way of control, which perhaps at that time did not make the minister's name popular at every fireside.
Then we come on to 1949-and I go quickly -when, under the influence of the British devaluation, we ourselves had to devalue. I wish to emphasize what happened from that time on, because I think it is both important and interesting. I should like to quote briefly what I said in the house in 1950. These were my words:
We have not advocated any sudden or violent step. We have not advocated a disregard of the fact that we have obligations under the Bretton Woods agreement. But what we have advocated is an approach to realism. Incidentally we believe-as I am sure the minister does also-that the course of events has put us in a strong position; our dollar is in a strong position.
The steps which preceded the action taken by the minister were rather interesting; because we find that in June the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), who is always very helpful, said, as reported at page 3185 of Hansard for June 5, 1950:
It is true at the moment Canadian funds are at a ten per cent discount from United States funds, but that may well be a temporary situation. The historic position of the Canadian dollar is at par with the United States dollar. How long the discount situation will continue, I do not know.

Later in the debate the Minister of Finance was asked if the Minister of Trade and Commerce was speaking for him, and his reply was that he was speaking for himself.
Then we come to September 2, 1950, when the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson) asked the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) this question:
In view of the statements in the press of Canada today, and questions being raised in both London and New York, and in order to clarify the exchange position and prevent the utmost confusion, can the Prime Minister indicate whether or not the government has any intention of altering the official exchange rate of the Canadian dollar in terms of United States dollars?
To that question the Prime Minister answered:
No consideration has been given to the matter referred to in the hon. member's question.
Then we remember the situation the Minister of Finance has already described-how there was an influx of American investment in September last. It is customary to refer to that as hot money, as if in some way that explained what happened. Actually it was an influx caused partly, of course, by speculation, in the belief that our dollar was too low, and partly by ordinary investment. At any rate the pressure became too great, and we know that on September 30 the minister changed the view which had been expressed so long by the government, and told us the dollar would be allowed to find its own level. It was difficult for the minister to do that, because it had been only a little more than a year before that the Prime Minister was reported to have said at Timmins, on May 26-and this appears in the Ottawa Citizen of May 27:
Mr. Drew's argument-
That is, his argument with regard to our position on the dollar.
-is a typical Tory proposal to benefit the few at the expense of the many.
Of course that was during an election campaign, and in such times we must not hold people too closely to everything they say. But just how it could be argued that the suggestion we made for realism in exchange-that is the word we used-was to benefit the few at the expense of the many, I do not know, and I doubt whether anyone else knows.
As I said, and as the minister has indicated, events became too strong, and the dollar was allowed to And its own level-which should have been done a long time before. What happened immediately was that it appreciated by nearly five cents, which of course meant that those people who had been buying goods in the United States,

such as coal, oil and the like, for a considerable time were injured by the fact that they had been using a dollar which, by the edict of the Department of Finance, was stated to be worth only ninety cents when actually the market showed on September 30, that it was worth about ninety-five cents.
Of course there was another very unfortunate incident. When you persist in wrong actions you sometimes have unexpected conclusions and evils resulting therefrom that you have not looked forward to. Of course the finance department did not expect that as a result of their action long before there would be some $200 million of new money, which the minister has referred to, injected into the Canadian currency, which still further debased our currency, diluted it, and of course just added more fuel to the fire and provided that much more money to send prices up just that much higher. If the dollar had been freed long before, as it should have been, that difficulty would not have arisen.
As I have said already, the minister has finally come to the point where he agrees with us, and he said in September last that the dollar would be allowed to find its own level. Now where do we stand? The minister has said very frankly that he regards the organization as a stand-by organization, but when we get into committee we shall have some questions to ask about the number of people still working for the foreign exchange control board, and about the amount of money which it costs. I think we may find questions in our minds as to whether this is not a fairly expensive stand-by organization.
What is it that remains for this organization to do now that the dollar, as the minister has said, has been set free on what we call current account, that is to say, in ordinary transactions of buying and selling? There is still a measure of control exercised over the movement of capital from Canada to the United States and vice versa. I would agree with the minister to this extent, that in this strange and troubled world it would be taking a good deal of responsibility to say that there must be no organization available in the event of some disaster or unexpected cataclysm which might disturb things.
As a matter of fact, since the dollar was allowed to find its own level the violent oscillations, the jumpings up and down of our holdings of United States exchange, which the minister referred to, have stopped. That is unless in the last month or two there has been a substantial change because, as the minister indicated, from the 30th of September when the change was made until the end of December the amount of United States
12, 1951
Foreign Exchange Control Act exchange remained level. That indicates that the dollar had found its proper level, that there was no unnatural movement of money. As a matter of fact, some have even suggested that there might again be a danger not of our having too little United States money but, with all the inducement there is to invest in our country now, of our even having too much United States money. It has even been suggested that we might need some kind of control available to stop an experience similar to what we had last September.
Of course there is one very obvious answer. Now that the dollar is free to find its own level, just as soon as you have United States money coming in here in any unusual amount it will raise the price of our dollar and it will tend to check itself in the natural, time-honoured and sensible way. Of course the same will be true about Canadian money going into the United States. Nevertheless, if the minister is coming and asking for some skeleton organization, some really stand-by organization, then it seems to me that we ought to be ready at any rate to take a good look at what he asks, but we are still hopeful that before the bill becomes law we shall be able to persuade the minister that no elaborate machinery is necessary.
I would carry the minister's mind back to the autumn of 1939. I think the minister would agree that, so far as permits covering ordinary travelling expenses for people going to the United States are concerned, there is no more need for the machinery we now have. I quite realize that the minister is relaxing it but there is no more need for that machinery than there is for machinery when you travel from Toronto to Montreal. As a matter of fact it almost looks as if, perhaps almost without intending it, the authorities were trying to keep people in the employ of the foreign exchange control board so as to have a full-fledged instrument if the need should arise again.
What I should like to point out to the minister, however, is that if capital controls are needed-and I think he will agree that is the only thing that is needed-those were made effective in September, 1939, with virtually no machinery except that of the Bank of Canada and the chartered banks. It will take a lot of persuasion even on the part of that persuasive man, the minister, to convince me that anything like what I imagine to be the number of staff in the foreign exchange control board is necessary. We will know more about that after we reach the committee stage.
Therefore what I would say is that, subject to what may come out in this debate and to

Foreign Exchange Control Act further investigation of the facts, I think it would be reasonable to have some stand-by organization to deal with unforeseen and perhaps even unimaginable difficulties that might arise. However, it would be very hard for me to believe that we need anything approaching the organization that we have had, and which is being kept busy now to some extent doing things which I think are utterly unnecessary.
There is one further point I should like to make. The question may be raised about our relationship to the international monetary fund. Many in this house Will recall that when the Foreign Exchange Control Act became law five years ago in 1946 one of the arguments made by the minister-and I think quite properly-was that it flowed from our membership in the international monetary fund. Attention has been drawn in this house by myself and others to the fact that as the years have gone by the authorities of the international monetary fund have been very emphatic in pointing out that they felt a growing measure of freedom-the very thing we advocated-should be brought into play. Of course it is clear that when that was done last September the international monetary fund accepted it, so far as I know, with good grace. That is another question which may arise but, Mr. Speaker, I say again that I still hope that we may have something much more simple without all the punitive powers that the foreign exchange control board has, because it seems to me there is nothing on the horizon to suggest that the ordinary mechanism which the minister in effect put into operation last September cannot serve for current account. There is also nothing to suggest why the Bank of Canada organization coupled with the mechanism of the chartered banks cannot be sufficient to deal with whatever measure of control of capital movement may be necessary.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words before the motion carries. I have listened with great interest today to the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell). I realize he is a former banker and is very familiar with foreign exchange and all the details connected therewith. I wish to take a few minutes to make a few remarks based on personal experiences I have had myself, and to say that I am strongly in support of the resolution. Since the Canadian dollar was allowed to seek its own level a few months ago it has been very noticeable that the margin between the rate of premium paid in the banks and the price charged Canadians requiring United States dollars has been very small. Previously, under arrangements not


of the same character, I have seen very wide margins between the buying and selling prices of United States dollars. As I have stated in this house on many occasions, I remember two periods-and incidentally they were both when we had Conservative governments here in Ottawa-when the difference between the buying and selling prices would be as high as six, eight and ten per cent. I may be wrong, but I have an idea the foreign exchange control board may be responsible for keeping these buying and selling prices very close, and I fear that if we discarded this board and had no way of controlling foreign exchange we might have the same condition we had during the first great war and in the early thirties.
I believe every Canadian should have the privilege of buying United States exchange at any time at a fair rate. In smaller towns we may have difficulties that are not found in larger cities. In a small town you may have only one bank; there is no competition, and conditions may be vastly different to those in larger cities. However, I do want to go on record as being very much in favour of this resolution. I believe the foreign exchange control board should be ready to function at any time circumstances demand it, and I believe many of the people in the section of the country from which I come are of the same opinion.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:

As I indicated in my statement, as a result of recent relaxations a person making a short trip to the United States can take up to $100 without an H form, as often as he wishes. With respect to selling merchandise in the United States the same practice will be followed that has prevailed in the past; the exporter must receive payment in United States dollars. I am not personally familiar with the details of the forms used. I know my hon. friend is,

because he has quite a large export business. As far as I am aware there is no change in the general practice with respect to merchandise exports. They must be invoiced and paid for in United States dollars.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: Then we still have to make out B forms for exports to bring back United States dollars in payment for those goods?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: Would the minister be able to say the amount involved in these travel moneys, if I may call them that? Is it substantial?

speechtext: The amount is very substantial. That has resulted in a very substantial additional demand for United States exchange. We expected that it would. We realized that the relaxation would be relatively expensive from the point of view of the loss of United States dollars, but we felt that our reserve position had reached a point where it was fully justified.

speechtext:
I understood that from now on this was going to be just a stand-by board. Foreign Exchange Control Act

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: Will the minister say whether the United States investor can take his capital gains out of the country? I understand he can take his dividends, but can he take capital gains?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: I do not think he can take out his capital gains, no. He can, of course, take current earnings out of the country. In the case of the removal of capital, whether it is capital which has been put in here or is an appreciation of capital assets, permission of the foreign exchange control board is required in order to take that capital out. I am not able to state offhand just what the attitude would be with respect to an individual transaction. The general rule is that in the case of capital which was in Canada prior to the inauguration of exchange control in 1939, that can only be taken out by special permission, and that permission would only be given in the light of general policy. After reading the statements of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), it seems clear that the statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce on May 30 still stands as a statement of fact, and that his statement of June 5 is also a statement of fact as of that date.

At page 17 of the report of the wheat board there are statistics for the quantities of Canadian wheat sold at various prices. I have done some calculations on the basis of those statistics. It is clear that during the four-year period we subsidized the Canadian consumer to the extent of $127-6 million.

One also could add to that the $48 million we subsidized the Canadian consumer prior to February 17, 1947. Then, by comparing the prices in the U.K. wheat agreement with the class 2 price for wheat, we subsidized the United Kingdom consumer in that four-year period to the extent of $380-2 million. This makes a total subsidy of both the Canadian and United Kingdom consumers of well over $500 million.
The wheat producers of western Canada are not asking the government to pay $500 million into the five-year pool; but they are determined that they will get more than the token payment of $65 million, which represents only 13 cents on the dollar. They feel they have good reason to ask a further substantial payment.
They have the statement of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) on August 15, 1946, in reply to the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) to the effect that while the government had provided $200 million for price support of agricultural products other than wheat, similar arrangements could be made for wheat, should the farmers' costs of production continue to increase.
The farmer has always asked and continues to ask for stability. But it is not good enough to stabilize wheat prices and then let the cost of production shoot higher and higher. On the basis of the statement of the Minister of Agriculture and other members of the government that not only would stabilization be applied to the price of wheat, but that through an orderly decontrol program we would not have inflation, I say the western wheat producers now have a claim for an additional payment over and above the 8-3 cents.
The western wheat producers have never agreed, and do not agree today, that they should be called upon to subsidize the Canadian consumer. They are opposed to subsidizing the Canadian consumer. They take the stand that if the Canadian consumer should get cheaper flour and cheaper bread, that subsidy should be paid out of the national treasury of the country, and that it should not be saddled on the backs of one particular group, namely the western wheat producer.
The Minister of Agriculture himself seems to have taken that position before, because, as reported at page 4806 of Hansard lor August 14, 1946, he said:

I agree with those who say that that whole cost should not be charged up to the farmer, and in discussions in the past I have maintained that too much of the cost has been charged up to the farmer. I still maintain that we should get away from that just as soon as we possibly can.
In agreeing to that five-year pool, the western wheat producer believed the statement of the Minister of Agriculture that the government was going to cease forcing the wheat producers to subsidize the Canadian consumer. Even today the wheat producer is forced to sell his wheat to the Canadian consumer for 25 cents a bushel less than the price of class 2 wheat.

That is the position at the moment.
I say on the basis of that statement alone the western wheat producers have an ironclad argument for the government making a further payment over and above the 8-3 cents a bushel.
Hon. members on all sides of the house realize that this is the hottest issue we have had to debate this session. The government must well know that the federation of agriculture in Saskatchewan, together with the executive of the western agricultural conference, have just had a meeting at Regina, and that they are sending a delegation to Ottawa to present to the government a unanimous submission on their behalf.
This is a hot political issue on the prairies. I say that if any prairie provincial government, Alberta, Saskatchewan or Manitoba, went to the country in 1951 the Liberal party would go down to overwhelming and disastrous defeat, on the basis of this wheat payment.
However, I do not wish to conclude on a political note, but I do want to ask the government to reconsider the decision with respect to 8-3 cents, and I make the plea that western prairie members who represent wheat constituencies, particularly my fellow M.P.'s in the Liberal party who come from Saskatchewan, should stand up and vote in favour of the C.C.F. subamendment calling for a final payment of 25 cents a bushel.

In any event that was the period he took; then he said right off the bat that would amount to $48 million, so the $166 million is now reduced to $118 million. If that is not pulling rabbits right out of the hat I should like to know what it is. The Canadian farmers lost $48 million just like that. That is quite a method of paying off the farmers. This may be a hot question, but it is going to be a hot proposition for the minister to prove that is a fair and equitable settlement to the farmers in western Canada.
Well, now we have it down to $118 million. Then listen to what the minister had to say:
If you take that figure then you find there is $48 million that should be deducted from losses in the first two years. That brings us down to $118 million. I went on to say:	We are not
going to attempt to prove that any figure short of a round figure is a reasonable figure to be asking under the terms of an agreement such as this, and therefore we are of opinion that $100 million would settle the bill.
So another $18 million goes out the window just like that. Surely no reasonable person, not even a Liberal sitting on the other side of the house, could agree to that. The $166 million has been reduced to $100 million

Canadian Wheat Board Act just like pulling a rabbit out of a hat. Then the minister had this to say:
Another proposal had been made that we might consider $70 million a settlement, and what I said at the end of my speech last night was that under the arrangement which was made for the final year there might have been a settlement of $35 million.
Let us see how the minister handles that $35 million. Of course this is the money of the farmers, and it is not very difficult to whittle it down. A little further on he said:
If you take into consideration the fact that we did get $1.98 a bushel for our wheat owing to the fact that there was devaluation of the pound, then the sum that we did obtain under that arrangement was $16 million and not $35 million.
So, owing to devaluation, all the farmers actually got was $16 million. The $35 million was settled for $16 million, and another $19 million went out the window. Well, if you take the $35 million and the $65 million the government has agreed to take out of the national treasury and put into the fund that makes the $100 million. So all that is left out of the $166 million will be the $16 million which came through devaluation and which was in the wheat board treasury, and the $65 million which is to be paid out of the national treasury. That is all they will get of the $166 million the minister figured was the actual loss. Then he had this to say in conclusion:
When you take all these facts into consideration, that we had asked $100 million, that they could claim, by having all the arguments on their side allowed, to have settled $35 million, there was still $65 million owing, and that $65 million has been paid.
Well, it was never paid by the British government. It was paid by the Canadian taxpayers, including the farmers. In other words the farmers are being taxed to pay themselves back. Then the minister went on, and this is the finest gem I have read for some time:
So far as the farmer is concerned it can be argued that the matter has been settled in the same manner as it would have been settled if Great Britain had made all the settlement that we asked them to make when we were in the midst of these discussions. I think that should be made clear to the house.
In other words, he says that we have just disregarded the $48 million to start with; we have whittled off another $16 million and then a further $19 million, and we have it down now to $65 million. He says that now everything is going to be fine. I do not think it is going to be fine. I do -not blame the farmers of western Canada for being greatly perturbed over the loss of this huge sum of money which they rightly had coming to them. When you recall that the actual loss to the farmers by reason of the United Kingdom agreement was $311,676,844, and then
IMr. Johnston.]
when you add to that, as the last speaker indicated, another $136,920,921 which was the loss on wheat sold to the millers in Canada, you find that the total loss amounts to $448,597,765. How can you expect agriculture to be satisfied with such an agreement?
You know, Mr. Speaker, it was rather amusing to read a statement attributed to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) in a newspaper dated March 8. I should like to put this statement on the record because I think it comes in at this point, particularly after this government has just finished chiselling the farmers to the extent I have indicated. This report appears in the Citizen of Thursday, March 8, and it reads:
Industry Farm Balances Urged by St. Laurent London, Ontario.-Keeping what he termed "proper balance" between Canada's agricultural progress and her industrial development was urged by Prime Minister St. Laurent in a surprise visit to the Middlesex seed fair and food show at Queen's park yesterday.
Canada, he noted, has been going ahead industrially "at a very rapid rate." Agriculture must keep pace because "a country is in a bad way if it cannot produce all the food it needs."
Proper distribution of food is also important "if agriculture is to continue as the cornerstone of the economy of this great nation," declared the Prime Minister.
How could he reasonably expect agriculture to continue to be the cornerstone of this great industrial nation when the government itself, through its policy, is the direct cause of the farmers losing $448 million? I believe we should be logical about the matter. Certainly, one cannot expect such a condition to continue.
Just before I left home to attend this session, I attended a meeting of the agricultural producers in Carbon, Alberta. It is not a large town, it is partly a mining town and partly agriculture. At any rate approximately 300 farmers attended the meeting and passed a resolution unanimously that the payment should be at least another 25 cents.
I have just received a letter from the farmers' union of Alberta at Carbon, local No. 1005, dated March 10 and reading as follows:
Dear Sir:
I am instructed by the above local to urge you to do all in your power to obtain the sum of 25 cents per bushel for the final payment of the five-year wheat pool. We feel that we farmers are actually entitled to more than this amount, yet will be satisfied if the dominion government agrees to pay out this sum, making up the balance of what is held at the moment by the Canadian wheat board with further moneys from the Canadian treasury.
Yours very truly,
Secretary-Treasurer.
When 300 farmers come out to a meeting in one of those small towns, the matter must be of some importance. You can well imagine that when we return home we are going to

have larger attendances at these meetings. This government is going to find that the farmers will not sit down and take it. Surely no respectable government would expect the agricultural industry to bear such a tremendous loss when it is remembered that during the last war other industries did not carry such losses. In fact, they did not carry any losses but were, in most cases, subsidized. When that is recalled and compared with what is happening to agriculture, there is just no reason in the attitude of this government.
When the war started there was legislation passed in this house to the effect that manufacturers' profits were limited to five per cent. I was a member of the war expenditures committee at that time. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) reported that he was not able to place one contract under that limitation, so the five per cent was raised. The very opposite action was taken with regard to agriculture. With world prices high, agricultural prices were forced down. It was through government action, and not the wheat board, that this wheat was sold at such a reduced price. It was a deliberate policy of this government. I was speaking at a meeting once when there were some Liberals present. They were objecting to these arrangements of the government for handling their wheat. I said to them, "I am sorry for those who did not vote Liberal, but you fellows who voted Liberal are getting just what you asked for". I think they are beginning to realize that. I believe that when the next election rolls around the other provinces will follow Alberta's example and clean house with the Liberals.

speechtext:
A message from His Excellency the Governor General transmitting estimates for the financial year ending March 31, 1952, was presented' by Hon. Douglas Abbott (Minister of Finance) and read by Mr. Speaker to the house.
Main Estimates, 1951-52 Hon. Douglas Abbott (Minister of Finance):
Mr. Speaker, I move:
That the message from His Excellency together with the estimates presented this day be referred to the committee of supply.
In doing so, I do not propose to make any lengthy statement, either in regard to the form of the estimates, in which there have been many changes in detail as a result of recommendations of the public accounts committee last year, or in regard to the figures. Instead I am following the practice that my predecessors and I have followed in past years of issuing a detailed statement to the press at the time the estimates are presented to the house. Copies of the statement will be available at my office for any member wishing to have one. Perhaps I might merely say, first, in regard to the form, that most of the suggestions of the public accounts committee have been adopted, and much more detail included. As a result, the volume is much larger-540 pages this year compared with 322 last year. Members will also find a pocket inside the back cover of this book, into which will fit a large table which is being printed separately and which will be available in two or three days, showing a cross classification of expenditures of various types in each department, as the committee recommended. As regards the figures themselves, the grand total of the estimates is, of course, much larger than this past year, because expenditures on defence and defence production have increased from about $770 million in this current year to $1,664 million in the new year-an increase of $894 million. The estimates for all other departments amount in total to approximately $1,923 million, compared with $1,958 million for the current year, including those supplementanes already appropriated. Thus we show a reduction for departments other than defence of $35 million, notwithstanding substantially higher levels of costs.
Motion agreed to.

speechtext: that the house go into committee of supply.

Before Your Honour leaves the chair, I wish to say a few words. Events of the past few months have seriously aggravated a situation which is itself rooted in both the domestic and international problems of the times. The grave unrest in the country today, coupled with the anxiety and uncertainty of all levels

Cost of Living
of production and trade, is reflected in this latest report from the bureau of statistics which came out the other day and which shows a sudden sharp increase in the cost of living over the previous month of 2 [DOT] 7 points, of almost 3 points.
It might be well to review the figures which have been published and which have become more or less familiar to all of us. Since 1945 the index has risen from 119-5 to 175-2, according to the latest calculation; and, judging toy the prices of consumer goods in the stores today, it is likely that they are considerably higher than that at the moment. It is significant that, where the monthly index fluctuated somewhat for the year 1949, showing a net increase of some 6-5 points, the year 1950 shows a record of steady increase, to close with a net increase of 9-6 points. Then we have the spectacle of the January report of this year showing an increase of 1 * 4 and the February report showing a further increase of 2-7.
It is my belief that one of the reasons for the sudden and sharp increase which was noted in this last report is the government's bland disregard of this situation and the feeling throughout the country that no one knows exactly where we are going. The February 1951 figures as released by the bureau of statistics show an increase of 13-6 over the same period for 1950. May I draw to the attention of the house the fact that the heaviest single monthly increases in 1950 were in the months of March and July. We are already well into March; and while I am aware that the figures which are reported are for the preceding month, I predict that the March report will follow the 1950 pattern, and probably the April one also.
As other costs rise, the cost of municipal administration rises with them; and the reports of local tax rates on real estate which have filled the newspapers this last month bear adequate testimony to the impact at the municipal level. All requirements of municipal services have been hit. All sorts of supplies, uniforms, cost of buildings, sewers, sidewalks and roads, as well as the necessary adjustments in wages, inadequate though they may be, have been added to the load. This in turn has provided an additional burden for the home owner and a further aggravation of the rental housing situation. Rather than help, this government, in the housing field alone, has aggravated the situation still further by the double-barrelled onslaught of the abolition of rent control and the curtailment of housing loans.
I hold no particular brief for the type of rent control which was in effect; for, like much government legislation, it was sadly in need of revision. Likewise, with the 
housing loans, the problem of supplies should have been met from an angle which would not have deprived the small income groups of the opportunity to purchase those houses which were available. In each case I suggest that the load might have been lightened by intelligent legislation rather than jettisoned. I predict further that the curtailment of mortgage loans will shortly result in increased demand for subsidized rental housing and that it will be found that the responsibility has not been lost but merely been shifted.
The average housewife today, whether or not she understands the economic pressures which contribute to the situation which we have, knows full well that her dollar will not buy her requirements. The pay envelope no longer keeps the family. She must deprive herself and her children of all of the luxuries and of many of the necessities of life or she must take the only alternative and go into debt.
Whether she is the wife of a farmer, a labourer or an industrial worker or whether the breadwinner in her family is in the great army of unorganized white-collar workers, is a small businessman, or is engaged in the practice of one of the professions, she knows the strain of trying to feed and clothe her family with an inadequate income. Some of these people have a moderate chance of increasing their income. Others have none at all. At the very top of the list of those who are helpless in the face of advancing costs are the pensioners and those who are trying to live on fixed incomes of one kind or another. To these people, many of them approaching the end of their lives, the picture is extremely dark indeed. It would seem to them, I am sure, that the only thing left for them to do is to depart this life altogether. But they are even afraid to die because the price of burials has also risen.
I am not making a morbid jest, Mr. Speaker;
I am extremely serious when I say that to those families, burdened with heavy medical and hospital costs and subsequent burial costs, the debt-ridden future looks black indeed. There is literally nothing that has not risen in price. This is the government's problem. This is the government's responsibility. This is no time for the pursuit of a policy of laissez-faire and it is no time for guessing. Theory does not feed hungry stomachs; it does not clothe bodies and it does not shelter families. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I urge on this government to withdraw its head from the sands of theoretical supposition and look upon this grim reality of current conditions and to take practical cognizance of the plight

of our families; and to this end, Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon):
That all the words after "that" to the end of the question be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"This house regrets that the government, in face of the continuing increase in the cost of living and particularly in the face of the recent sharp rise thereof, refuses to take effective measures to protect the Canadian family budget."
Amendment negatived on division.

REDUCTION IN URBAN MAIL DELIVERIES
speechtext:
Before the main motion is adopted there is another matter that I want to discuss in the house, namely, the matter pertaining to the new system that is being inaugurated by the Post Office Department. As we all know, the Post Office Department has recently inaugurated a one-a-day delivery in cities and urban areas that heretofore have been receiving a two-a-day delivery service.
Generally speaking, I think the Canadian people will approve of any move made by the government to economize in the government's service, particularly in this critical period. The question does arise, though: why should the Post Office Department be the first department in which the government chooses to exercise that policy? The Post Office Department is the first department in which we have the application of that policy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: REDUCTION IN URBAN MAIL DELIVERIES
speechtext: It is only a little more noticeable there.

subtopic: REDUCTION IN URBAN MAIL DELIVERIES
speechtext:
And it is the one department of government that differs from others, in that it is paid for directly by the public. It is a public service for which those who use the mails pay. It is not a department that like other departments is a drain upon the public treasury; and we question whether the government, which in past years has shown a profit in the post office of I think something over $12 million, which was reduced last year to something more than $2 million, is really justified in operating the Post Office Department at a profit. The question arises as to just what justification there is for a government taking out of the users of the mail service a profit to that extent.
I presume it is because there was a drop in profits last year that the government is now attempting to reduce the service. It seems to me to be poor business to be paying the Trans-Canada Air Lines, and other air lines, what I think amounts to about three times the rate charged by the rail services to fly 80709-75
Postal Service
mail into our large cities, and to leave that mail lying for twenty-four hours or more in the post office without being delivered, as will be the case under the present system.
There are in my riding a great many of those walks which, while they do not contain more than twenty-five per cent business calls, do contain a great many business calls, and businessmen who have their offices on the residential streets, organizations which maintain their offices on those residential streets, are already complaining, and I think quite fairly, of the service.
I have a letter here from one organization which carries on business across this province, and which receives a great deal of mail during the day. During the past week it has been getting its mail after 6.30 every evening. That is not good service, and no private company would put up with that kind of service for a moment.
Apart altogether from the service to the public there is the effect of this service upon the postmen employed. This is a rather important topic into which I want to go at some length, Mr. Speaker, and I should like you to call it six o'clock.
