subtopic: REDUCTION IN URBAN MAIL DELIVERIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before six o'clock I had raised the question as to why the government had phosen to inaugurate its economy policy in the one department of government that was being paid for by the users of that service, rather than being paid for out of general taxation, I now have before me the minister's report for the year ended March 31, 1949, and I find that since 1932 there has been one year only in which that department did not show a net surplus. That net surplus amounted in 1944 to $12,500,000. It dropped to $9,800,000 in 1948 and to $2,900,000 in 1949. I find that the drop from 1948 to 1949 was due in the first instance to the fact that about $5,600,000 had been spent on increased salaries. However I find also that there was an increase of $1,800,000 paid to Trans-Canada Air Lines for the inauguration of the so-called all-up service.

subtopic: REDUCTION IN URBAN MAIL DELIVERIES
REDUCTION IN URBAN MAIL DELIVERIES
speechtext:
In 1948-49. I understand that Trans-Canada Air Lines charged $1.81 per ton mile for the carrying of mail, which is just about three times as much as they charge for the carrying of express and cargo traffic. I suggest that if the department wanted to economize in post office

Postal Service
expenditures, pressure should have been brought to bear on Trans-Canada Air Lines to reduce their charges for the carrying of mail to something approximating their express and cargo traffic charges.
Then, I notice in a report given by the deputy postmaster general, Mr. Turnbull, before the transport and communications committee last March that the post office last year had a deficit of $8 million due to the fact that the postage rate on periodicals is less than the cost of making delivery. It may well be that it would be in the national interest for the Canadian government to subsidize magazine publishers-possibly Canadian magazine publishers. I can well understand the difficulty the publishers of Canadian magazines may have, particularly when they are in competition with American magazines. But I doubt the wisdom of making the users of the mail service pay those subsidies-and certainly anything which would subsidize foreign magazines. If it is necessary to subsidize Canadian magazines, then I suggest that it should be paid as a direct subsidy, and not charged up against those who use the mails.
I suggest that before the government undertook to curtail this service to the public, for which the public is making direct payment, it should have investigated other ways and means of economizing within the department. I believe there is good ground for criticism in the way this new policy regarding mail delivery was introduced. As I understand it a blanket order was issued, applicable across the country, whereby a postman is required to take his own route, and either a half or a third of an adjoining route.
I suggest that any well-managed industry, before undertaking a change in policy as drastic as that, one which would affect the public and employees to the extent this change does, would have carried out some experiments. It would have found out, through experiments, just how the new policy would work, and what difficulties would be encountered. I believe that if the government had taken any one postal district in any one of our larger cities, and spent a month or two in attempting to work out the new delivery system, it would not have found it feasible to add one-half or one-third of one route to another route, and making delivery once a day, without overburdening the postman or requiring him to work more than a forty-four-hour week. I believe the department would have discovered that such a blanket order could not have been put into effect without to a very great extent disrupting a service universally recognized across the country as one of our most efficient government services.

For a few moments I should like to speak about the effect of this change upon mail carriers- Hon. members have read in the press about mass meetings of postmen in a number of our larger cities. Some of us in the house had the opportunity of attending one of those mass meetings in Toronto. There we were told that postmen in all the Toronto postal districts had kept an accurate check of the hours they had had to work the previous week in order to complete their deliveries. Many of them, instead of having to work forty-four hours as they were supposed to do, worked up to as much as sixty hours. I hold in my hand a report from one postal district in Toronto. Even before the change I find that every man in that postal district was working from one to two hours over and above the forty-four-hour week. The shortest week worked in that district before the change was made was forty-eight hours. The average for the entire district having 23 routes was not 44 hours a week before the change but 49 hours and 53 minutes, nearly 50 hours a week before any change was introduced when they were still supposed to be working 44 hours.
Last week, with the new system in operation, the 27 postmen in that district worked an average of 52J hours instead of 44. There are just two points I want to raise in that connection. In addition to the longer hours there is the extra amount of mail that has to be delivered during the day. Every report that I have been able to secure indicates that the postmen are required to carry considerably more than the regulation weight of mail. They are working longer hours, and the majority of these postmen are great war veterans. Many of them are veterans of the first world war who have been in the service of the Post Office Department for 20 years or more. They are finding the extra load and the extra hours extremely difficult.
There is the further fact that they are required to work four or five hours a day over their eight-hour day through no fault of their own. These extra hours are thrown upon them because of the department's policy in inaugurating this new system of delivery. They were raising no objection to having to go to the post office an hour before starting time in order to get their mail ready for their routes. None of them raised any objection to working 48 or 50 hours instead of 44 under the old system. Now they are required to work 53 to 60 hours. In all fairness, if the government is to deal with these employees as fairly as it expects industry and employers generally to deal with their employees, then the government owes it to these men to pay them for that extra time.

I raised that question in the house this afternoon on the orders of the day and was told that as yet the government has given no consideration to paying for these extra hours. For two weeks the Toronto stations have been on the new system. It will probably take many more weeks before the routes are adjusted to a point where delivery can be made in an eight-hour day. Until such time as that takes place I submit that these extra hours should be paid for by the government. I think it is entirely unfair to throw upon thousands of employees delivering mail for the Post Office Department anywhere from five to ten extra hours a week through no fault of their own, simply because the department inaugurated the system without having properly worked out the details or knowing what the effect of the application of the system would be. I suggest that the government should take into consideration payment for the extra time worked.

subtopic: REDUCTION IN URBAN MAIL DELIVERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words on this subject. I find it hard to understand why the letter carriers of the Post Office Department were picked on in the way that they have been in this drive for economy. It may be because the Postmaster General is a new minister. Others may be taking advantage of the fact that he is a junior member of the cabinet, is perhaps a little reluctant to argue with the older members, and so forth. 'That is the only reason I can see because in dealing with price controls the government says there is no emergency, and if and when there is an emergency they will implement the emergency powers. Second, in the matter of defence production the same thing is true. The government is taking stand-by legislation in case they may have to use it.
In speaking about the possibilities of war in the foreseeable future the Prime Minister has said, outside this house of course, that he believes there is no immediate danger of over-all war, that he expects to live a long time and does not expect to see an over-all war in his lifetime. That is all very reassuring but the government then decide that they must cut drastically civilian spending, the ordinary expenditures of government. They say that we have to offset in some way the huge defence expenditures that we are now making because we may have to face a conflict some time in the future.
So far as I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, I am in agreement with the government on its drive to institute measures that will reduce as far as possible, without impairing the services of the country, any department of the government that is considered nonessential. I cannot understand, however, and I cannot go along with the government in 80709-75J
Postal Service
picking on the letter carriers, who represent about the lowest status in the postal department.
Who are these letter carriers? The great majority of them across this country are veterans of the first war. Many of them are disability pensioners. They are reaching an age when in a few years they will be retiring on the maximum pension paid under the civil service. Many of these men have made commitments. They have bought homes. They have planned their lives so that they may be able to eke out an existence on their pensions if and when they are retired. This economy measure of the government is resulting in the dismissal from the service of many of these older men. They will have to take their pensions prematurely which will mean a lot less than they anticipated on the basis of being able to work out their terms of service.
That is one angle. Second, the minister and others have created the impression at least that they are reducing the work, that they are cutting down the number of deliveries. Cutting down the number of deliveries is not reducing the work. You are going to carry exactly the same amount of mail but you are going to have twelve hundred fewer letter carriers across the country to make deliveries. The figures I have seen in the press indicate that approximately twelve hundred mail carriers are to be laid off. I think I would be safe in saying that the great majority of these fellows will be the older personnel, from the first war; and even if they are young men it does not alter the picture. The result is exactly the same; the same amount of mail will be carried by just that many fewer letter carriers across the country, which means that the load will have to be increased.
I am not arguing at all for the continuation of two or three mail deliveries a day. One delivery a day is good enough for me, as I think it is good enough for almost everyone in this country. I am arguing against picking on those with the very lowest status in the department, men who are absolutely essential, men who have been accepted into the civil service and have planned their lives accordingly. At a moment's notice, because of a hypothetical emergency which is not recognized in any other government department, these men are to have their lives interrupted and all their plans for the future disrupted.
I do not think that can be justified. If the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) came in and said he was going to cut his office staff across the country by fifty per

Postal Service
cent, I would say perhaps he was justified. That would not hurt anyone very much. II the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Prudham) came in and said he was going to wipe out a certain branch for the duration of the war I would1 say perhaps that could be justified, that no one would suffer very much and perhaps it would not even be noticed, though of course he would have to keep on the geologists because they are very busy people. I would not argue with economy measures of that kind for the purpose of increasing defence production and providing the necessary office staff for the new department. But I am strongly arguing against picking on men in the mail carrier category, because I think they are essential. They have rendered good service for many years, and I do not think the government can justify the adoption of a policy, without consultation with the civil service organizations, which uproots so many of these employees.
I suggest to the Postmaster General (Mr. Rinfret) that he take another look at it. He is not going to save very much money by penalizing the letter carriers, but in my opinion he is going to create a great deal of resentment across the country. Then when he comes to resume this service he may have a great deal of difficulty getting the necessary employees, because I should think anyone treated this way would hesitate before accepting service with a branch of the government which pulled that kind of thing on their predecessors. Personally I think this is about the meanest cut that could be made. Others can defend themselves. Men with ability in certain directions can be shifted from one department to another, or they can be let out. They can always rehabilitate themselves. But when you take a mail carrier and throw him in the street you are putting him in the ranks of the unemployed, and it is very doubtful if you will ever get him back into government service. In view of the small amount of money that will be saved and the hardship and injustice that will be created, I suggest that the Postmaster General take another look and leave the letter carrier service as it was.

subtopic: REDUCTION IN URBAN MAIL DELIVERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had hoped to bring up this matter on the estimates, but since the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) has raised it this evening I should like to say a word or two. The two previous speakers have dealt with the general situation, and I should like to bring to the attention of the Postmaster General (Mr. Rinfret) the situation in my own city.
While I appreciate the need for economy in this direction, I think perhaps economy can be overdone if it interferes with the efficiency

and comfort of the employees. My information is that in Saskatoon some 580 hours of overtime were worked in 24 days in February. The weather in Saskatoon in February is rather difficult, and I am informed that these men carried out that overtime work under a great deal of strain. The overtime was done on 24 routes; I am not clear on the matter, but I understand the men are not going to be compensated for the extra overtime work they performed under the strain I have indicated. In spite of the fact that this overtime had to be put in, six carriers have been released; and under those conditions I think they are quite justified in protesting those dismissals.
Like the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) I had the case of an elderly man who had only fourteen months to go until he reached the normal retirement age of 65. Mr. Speaker, in common with all the hon. members representing urban constituencies, I too have been receiving complaints about the economy program instituted by the Post Office Department. Perhaps I have received more complaints about the way in which economies were being made than about the economies themselves. May I say immediately that I am not opposed to the government starting on an economy campaign. I believe that, over the service as a whole, there is a great deal that could be done, and that perhaps there is a great need of an economy campaign. I do object, however, to the campaign starting with the little fellow. I think the campaign should not start right at the bottom, but it should start at the top and work down.
For the moment, let me deal with the way this thing has been put before me. I am told that the organizations of letter carriers were not consulted before the changes were made. They were simply told. In every industrial establishment today the working conditions are arrived at by agreement between the employees, who have an organization, and the employer. If there is to be a change in those working conditions then the employees, as people of importance because they do the work, are consulted. The change is made by mutual consent. I am told that is not the way this change has been made. The post office officials carried out a reorganization and said that instead of working for forty-eight hours tomorrow you shall work fifty-four hours from tomorrow forward. If a private employer treated his employees in that fashion in this country there would be an uproar because an ordinary self-respecting workman would not stand for that sort of treatment. I suggest that, although it is too late to do it in the proper way this time, at any other time when there is a reorganization of this kind contemplated the representatives of those who are doing the work should be consulted. Remember, the important people in every organization or in every line of work are those who do the work, because the work cannot be done without them. The services of the community

Postal Service
cannot be carried on without them and they should have some say in how their work is arranged.
There is no need for me to repeat what has been said by the hon. members for York South (Mr. Noseworthy), Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) and Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green). The problems in all the cities are pretty much the same, and I do deplore the way the Post Office Department has set about this reorganization.

I listened with considerable interest to the discussion and to the criticisms which have been voiced by the members who have spoken about this matter tonight. I should like to point out to those who come from the urban parts of Canada that this problem with which they are being faced now, that is the treatment of letter carriers in urban centres, is not new for those of us who come from the rural parts of Canada. We have been experiencing this, I sometimes think, with less than the sympathy we deserve from many parts of the dominion who ought to be just as interested in rural mail deliveries as we are in the urban deliveries.
While it is perhaps repeating arguments that have been used many times in the past, nevertheless so long as the condition exists I take it that there will have to be on all sides of the house champions to bring the Post Office Department to its senses. This is just another example of the way the department of the Postmaster General (Mr. Rinfret) has been running wild with regard to its organization and its treatment of those who do its work. On many occasions I pointed out to the minister and to his predecessors in office that I felt there was no justifiable excuse for not giving this parliament a special committee set up to deal with the Postmaster General's department. I then had in mind, of course, more particularly the question of the scandalous returns which are given to the rural mail couriers across the country. It is all very well to say that they are under contract; but that does not excuse the governmental sin of underpayment, even though they are under contract. Today there are many hundreds and perhaps thousands of rural mail couriers who are carrying the mails to rural mail boxes at less than the cost of operating, calculated on any kind of a business basis. When, in addition to that, I now hear complaints as to the way the department is operating in the urban areas, and when you add to that the fact that we badly need some kind of policy with respect to the suburban areas, I am confirmed in my opinion. In between the urban and the rural sections there has now grown up in many [Mr. MacInnis.J
parts of Canada, almost like a mushroom, a great suburban section of our population. Mail delivery is a matter of great inconvenience to some of them, because they have come out of the cities where they have been accustomed to urban delivery. They are now in the position where they are obliged to go long distances in order to get to their mail boxes or to their post office in the new place to which they have gone. As the minister must know, there is no end to the complaints with respect to the lack of proper servicing of those people in the new areas.
I want to say this to the minister, and' I say it with every constructive motive. I think he ought to pause and consider just where the Postmaster General's department is heading with respect to rural, suburban and urban areas. If there ever was a department that at any time needed to have a first-class review of what it is doing, I think it is the Postmaster General's department now. It is all very well for the minister to suggest that after all they are part of the great economy wave. The waves do not seem to be so high in other departments. I know of no reason why an economy drive should not be tempered with common sense; because, after all, economy without common sense results in a policy of penny wise and pound foolish. The fact that, as the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) has so well put it tonight, they have picked upon the little man in the government service seems to me to be a good indication that there is a lack of common sense and good judgment in dealing with these matters. I suggest to the minister that, not only in debates on rural mail couriers but also with regard to complaints with respect to our suburban sections and now this acute criticism which has come to the government-and justifiable, if I may say so-with respect to the letter carriers in urban sections, enough evidence has been adduced, here to warrant us in demanding, before we go any further, that a special committee of this house be set up to review the way in which the Postmaster General's department is being operated'. I should think the minister would welcome that suggestion. I warn him that the public relations of the Postmaster General's department are rapidly deteriorating as a result of the manner in which it is being operated1 throughout the country. It is surely a department that is not so difficult to operate; because in many cases the public works department has in the past been providing the facilities in which it works. It has been receiving a revenue which enables it to operate and show a net profit generally on its year's operations. It seems to me that it should not be such a difficult department to administer that it should find itself in difficulties with respect

to urban, suburban and rural areas of the dominion. I am going to suggest to the minister that, before he goes any further, he ought to recommend) to this house that we have a special committee to deal with the Postmaster General's department and to see just where we are headed1. Before that committee we could call to give evidence those who ought to know perhaps better than most of us in the House of Commons do, namely the people who are affected: both those who are the customers of the department and those who are employed by it. Those are things that I think ought to form the basis for the setting up of a committee now. If the minister in previous sessions did not think that our arguments, when they dealt with rural mail couriers alone, carried sufficient weight to justify the setting up of a committee, surely, with the suburban and urban difficulties heaped upon the rural mail difficulties, there is now no justification for not giving parliament a special committee to deal with these matters. When a committee is set up I fancy that the minister will find that he will have a new and better perspective of just what is required in connection with the work of the department. In many respects the department has been a good one, but it is now getting into the position where, it seems to me, it is running wild; and I think it is about time that parliament took some steps to tame it before it gets completely out of bounds.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EARLY DISTRIBUTION OF PAYMENTS AT END OF POOL PERIOD, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, now everyone can relax because we are going to get back to the very soothing subject of wheat.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EARLY DISTRIBUTION OF PAYMENTS AT END OF POOL PERIOD, ETC.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EARLY DISTRIBUTION OF PAYMENTS AT END OF POOL PERIOD, ETC.
speechtext:
When I opened the debate on second reading of Bill No. 5 I said I did not intend to enter into a discussion of the five year pool which, of course, has nothing to do with the proposed amendments to the Canadian Wheat Board Act. In view of the debate that has taken place, however, I think I should make some further remarks at this point.
Attempts have been made by opposition speakers to prove: (1) that returns to western farmers from the five year pool were unsatisfactory; (2) that the British wheat agreement should not have been entered into.
An attempt has also been made to distort the facts about the attitudes taken by the Canadian and the United Kingdom governments with respect to the fulfilment of the agreement.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EARLY DISTRIBUTION OF PAYMENTS AT END OF POOL PERIOD, ETC.
speechtext: Who made that attempt?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EARLY DISTRIBUTION OF PAYMENTS AT END OF POOL PERIOD, ETC.
speechtext:
I intend to show that the arrangements in effect during the five years under discussion were in the interests of the western wheat farmer, and that without these arrangements the situation today would be very much less satisfactory than it is. I intend to show that the Canadian and British 

governments entered into an agreement that was beneficial to both the Canadian producer and the British consumer, and that the terms of that agreement were fully observed on both sides.
However, I am not going to argue that if we could have foreseen in 1945 what was going to happen in the following five years we should have done exactly what we did.
I am sure we should have done some things quite differently. That is the advantage of hindsight, upon which members of the opposition lean so heavily. Nevertheless I firmly believe that in 1945 and 1946 the government took decisions which were fundamentally sound, and that have contributed to the stability and prosperity of the wheat growers. It is possible to calculate by some elaborate guesswork that a higher average price might have been obtained over the four year period had there been no British agreement, but these are hypothetical calculations. They are based on conjecture and not on fact.
The only solid fact in this present situation is that over a five year period the wheat grower realized an average return of about $1.83 per bushel for No. 1 northern wheat in store Fort William. When in the history of Canada has the wheat grower ever enjoyed such consistently high returns over such an extended period? Certainly not in the period between 1930 and 1935 when this country was governed by the Conservative party.

When the hon. members of the Progressive Conservative party are making calculations about supposed losses under the British agreement they might try to calculate the losses suffered by western wheat growers during the early thirties when their party was responsible for wheat marketing. My hon. friend does not market western wheat very much. He does not know very much about it. The five year pool and the British agreement were an experiment in long-term stability. They were entered into

at a time of uncertainty at the end of world war II. No one knew what would happen. As I listen to the parties opposite criticizing the results of the five year pool I recall their attitude in this house. Could anyone at the end of the war have been more fearful of the future than the two main opposition groups in this house? As I remember it, they were predicting blue ruin.
But now, with the advantage of hindsight, they shift their position. Now they say that the government was wrong to strive for stability in markets. Now they say or imply that we should have refused to enter into an agreement with the British government assuring reasonable prices and an assured market over a four year period.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EARLY DISTRIBUTION OF PAYMENTS AT END OF POOL PERIOD, ETC.
speechtext: If I may interrupt, we did not say that; we supported the agreement when it was made.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EARLY DISTRIBUTION OF PAYMENTS AT END OF POOL PERIOD, ETC.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EARLY DISTRIBUTION OF PAYMENTS AT END OF POOL PERIOD, ETC.
speechtext: I have said nothing about the losses.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EARLY DISTRIBUTION OF PAYMENTS AT END OF POOL PERIOD, ETC.
speechtext: You have not but some of your followers have had a good deal to say about it. I think I said before, and I say again, that the time when you must decide whether an agreement is good or bad is when you sign on the dotted line, and we signed on that dotted line in 1946. That is when the decision had to be made and that is when it was made.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EARLY DISTRIBUTION OF PAYMENTS AT END OF POOL PERIOD, ETC.
speechtext: It is nice to know your fellows all like it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EARLY DISTRIBUTION OF PAYMENTS AT END OF POOL PERIOD, ETC.
speechtext:
The government did not share the unreasonable fears of the opposition parties about the future. But when an opportunity arose to sell 600,000,000 bushels of wheat at assured prices to our best customer -more than had ever before been sold by Canada to that customer 'in any comparable period-we accepted. That decision was supported by the great majority of the western wheat growers and I am confident that they still support it. Everyone recognized that there were risks in such an agreement. There were risks on both sides. But it must never be forgotten that there were even greater risks in not entering into the agreement. The advantage of the agreement was that it minimized the risk. The wheat agreement was similar to an insurance policy. Because a man who buys an accident policy never claims under it that does not mean the policy should not have been taken out, or that the premiums should not have been paid. It is well to keep that in mind. If wheat prices in the last two years had fallen very substantially the shoe would have been on the other foot, and I do not think it would have been proper for the United Kingdom to ask us to accept
Canadian Wheat Board Act less than the floor prices provided in the agreement in order to reduce average returns to the open market level.
As I shall point out later, the have regard to clause is important but it did not mean, and we have never argued that it meant, that the United Kingdom should make up in the final two years any mathematical calculation of losses in the first two years. Five years ago the western wheat grower supported a policy of stability at reasonable prices. Today, unless I am seriously mistaken, he still supports that policy. There are some, however, who do not believe in the policy of stability at reasonable prices. Some of those people are today criticizing the five year pool and the British agreement. I suggest to those who now think they see an opportunity of gaining some political advantage by attacking the government on the results of the five year pool and the British agreement that they should consider carefully whether they are not playing into the hands of those who prefer to return to the old boom and bust type of wheat marketing.
The test of any policy is its results; and I believe the results of a policy which returned an average of $1.83 a bushel on the basis of No. 1 northern in store Fort William for nearly 1 [DOT] 5 billion bushels of wheat sold over a five year period require no apology; and I am making none. The wheat economy prospered during that period as it deserves to prosper and as I hope and believe it will continue to prosper. If a policy can produce that kind of result it meets the only test that matters. The essential fact is that producers are being paid on the basis of $1-833 on their deliveries for five successive crops.
Let us look at the relevant facts about wheat marketing in each of the five years. In September, 1945, my predecessor, Hon. James MacKinnon, announced an export price of $1.55 a bushel until further notice, together with the government's undertaking that returns to producers would not be permitted to fall below $1 per bushel for the next five years. This policy was the genesis of the five year pool which was announced the following July when the contract with the United Kingdom was signed. As a result of the five year pool producers are receiving $1.83 per bushel, basis No. 1 northern, on all deliveries of about 235 million bushels during the 1945-46 crop year. The final payment is 28-3 cents over the export price of $1.55 which remained in effect during that year, and is well above the open market price in other countries. The average prices received on the farm in the United States during the 1945-46 crop year was $1.49 a bushel. The man who grew wheat and marketed it in this

Canadian Wheat Board Act pool in 1945-46 did1 not lose very much. Obviously he gained 28 cents per bushel over any other method of marketing.
Coming now to the first two years of the contract, the crop years 1946-47 and 1947-48, again the essential fact is that the producers are receiving $1.83 on 335 million bushels delivered in the 1946-47 crop year and on 244 million bushels delivered in the 1947-48 crop year. These turned out to be years of acute shortage of wheat in the world, and admittedly exorbitant prices could be obtained for marginal quantities in marginal markets. It should be recalled', however, that in order to finance the necessary imports of the United Kingdom, including wheat, the United, States loaned the United Kingdom $3,750 million and Canada also loaned the United Kingdom $1,250 million. The bulk of these loans were utilized more rapidly than anyone anticipated. Any higher prices charged for wheat would have ground down those loans more rapidly. As it was, the situation could only be met adequately by the Marshall aid program the United States placed in operation in 1947.
I think it is a fair question to ask those who are claiming that the producers lost money in those first two years of the contract: from what source additional payments, in the absence of a contract, might have come? Even in those years, when the United States government supported their domestic wheat prices, and exported wheat without payment, the prices American producers received at the farm were $1.90 and $2.29 in the two crop years respectively. Our own efforts to extend credits and accommodate our overseas buyers during this period, as hon. members are well aware, resulted in such a loss in exchange that we had to adopt rigid exchange conservation measures.
From 1947 to 1949 the United States permitted Marshall aid funds to be used for the purchase of Canadian wheat, and though large stocks of wheat were accumulating in the United States that government respected the United Kingdom-Canada agreement and did not demand that the Marshall aid funds be used to purchase United States wheat instead of Canadian wheat. However, before the 1949 crop came on the market United States wheat was declared in surplus supply, which automatically stopped the use. of Marshall aid funds to buy Canadian wheat. Just think of the importance of that agreement during those years. Because of the agreement, the United States paid money to Canada for supplying wheat to Britain, instead of giving away her own surplus wheat to England, at a time when the surplus in the United States was becoming burdensome. Those who are

making up the equation to show losses might very well put in that intangible for a very considerable price indeed.
Passing on now to the 1948-49 crop year, which was the third year of the contract, producers will receive $1.83 for deliveries of 293 million bushels. Throughout this crop year the payment difficulties of the United Kingdom continued acute. To put it bluntly what we faced here in Canada was the very real possibility that the United States would drive Canadian wheat out of our traditional markets. This actually occurred in the European markets with the exception of the United Kingdom, and the fact is that the Canada-United Kingdom wheat agreement was of the greatest value at this time in retaining our position in the United Kingdom market. As a matter of fact we have a very serious problem ahead of us in regaining markets in continental Europe which are now being supplied by the United States under Marshall aid. It was for that reason the government sent a mission to Europe last year for the express purpose of finding out how to regain a foothold in some of those markets. What the Canada-United Kingdom wheat agreement actually accomplished was to enable us to hold our position in the United Kingdom market. The United States government respected the agreement, and in fact went so far as to provide a very substantial amount of United States dollars, $175 million to be exact, which enabled the United Kingdom to finance her wheat purchases from the 1949 wheat crop under the agreement. This amount was provided as the result of negotiations which took place in Washington early in September, 1949. In evidence of those negotiations let me quote from a letter of September 13, 1949, from Mr. Paul G. Hoffman, economic co-operation administrator, to Hon. Charles F. Brannan, United States secretary of agriculture:
Dear Mr. Secretary:
As you know, one of the measures proposed by the United Kingdom during the three-power financial conferences was the financing with ECA grant funds of the British requirements for wheat from Canada.
The facts, with which you are familiar, are these:
The United Kingdom is the traditional and normal outlet for the major portion of wheat exported by Canada. Three years ago these countries entered into an agreement under which the United Kingdom was to purchase 140 to 160 million bushels of wheat annually from Canada. The quantity of wheat involved for 1949-50, the final year covered by the agreement, is 140 million bushels at an agreed price of $2 a bushel in store Fort William. The total dollar f.a.s. cost of the wheat involved for 1049-50 amounts to $309 million.
You have on several occasions advised us that wheat is a surplus agricultural commodity under the provisions of section 112 (d) of the Foreign Assistance Act, 1048, and it is my understanding that this

condition still prevails. Effective with delivery after the first calendar quarter of 1949, the ECA discontinued authorizing the use of its funds for the purchase of Canadian wheat, and as a consequence, the United Kingdom has been using its free dollar reserves to meet the deficit in its Canadian accounts, a substantial element of which consists of Canadian wheat.
Recently, there has been a very severe drain on United Kingdom gold and dollar reserves. This drain, if not halted, would quite certainly vitiate the progress towards economic rehabilitation and recovery which the United Kingdom has made and remove all prospects of achieving the objectives of the Foreign Assistance Act, not only in the United Kingdom but in all probability in the other countries participating in the European recovery program. It is, therefore, a vital necessity to take all steps possible to end the drain on British gold and dollar reserves.
In an effort to avoid this grave contingency and to extend such help as is within our power, we propose, under the provisions of the Foreign Assistance Act, to agree in part to the British proposal and authorize the use of $175 million of ECA grant funds to finance a portion of this year's purchases of Canadian wheat by the United Kingdom. Aside from the vital importance of such action to European recovery, we believe that the proposed action is also in the interests of agricultural producers in this country, in that it will not result in any over-all decrease in U.S. wheat exports and will facilitate additional exports of other agricultural commodities, both to Canada and the United Kingdom.
In weighing the losses under the agreement, let them weigh in the $175 million supplied by the government ini the United States to pay Canada for wheat shipped to Britain, which it is very probable Britain could not have bought without that assistance. Incidentally that assistance was barred under the strict terms of the Marshall aid plan.
Mr. Speaker, I can well imagine how the members of the opposition would have denounced the government if Canada had been pushed out of the United Kingdom market in 1948-49 and 1949-50 by Marshall aid wheat. I can testify personally, for I took part in the negotiations, that such a result most certainly would have occurred without the British wheat agreement.
In completing this survey of our marketing situation throughout the five year pool, I should mention the developments during the 1949-50 crop year in which producers will have received $1.83 per bushel on deliveries of 320 million bushels. As I have already mentioned, our sales in that crop year to the United Kingdom were partly financed by ECA funds. We had a firm sale to the United Kingdom of 145 million bushels at a price of $2 per bushel, which was 20 cents per bushel more than the international wheat agreement price for that year. This assured market was very important to us in a year in which we found some difficulty in finding other markets for the balance of our exportable supplies. In fact, we carried into the present
Canadian Wheat Board Act crop year some wheat supplies that would have moved earlier, had we been able to find markets for them. Again, I say the British wheat agreement needs no apology. It was the right thing to do at the right time. It was by no means a one-sided contract. It was beneficial to the Canadian wheat grower as well as to the British consumer.
Now I come to the third point, whether or not the British government lived up to the terms of the agreement. At the risk of some repetition, let me review the terms of the agreement and the course of negotiations between the Canadian and United Kingdom governments. As hon. members know, the agreement called for the delivery of 160 million bushels of wheat and flour during each of the crop years 1946-47 and 1947-48 at a base price of $1.55 per bushel for No. 1 northern, in store Fort William-Port Arthur. During each of the two final years a quantity of 140 million bushels was involved at prices to be negotiated. In 1948-49 the price was to be not less than $1.25 per bushel and in 1949-50 not less than $1 per bushel.
I now quote from the agreement itself. I should like to fix this have regard to clause in everyone's mind so it will not be misquoted as it has been on almost every occasion on which it has been mentioned:
The actual prices to be paid for wheat to be bought and sold' within the crop year 1948-49 shall be negotiated and settled between the United Kingdom government and the Canadian government not later than the 31st December, 1947, and prices for wheat to be bought and sold within the crop year 1949-50 shall be negotiated and settled not later than the 31st December, 1948. In determining the prices for these two crop years, 1948-49 and 1949-50, the United Kingdom government will have regard to any difference between the prices paid under this agreement in the 1946-47 and 1947-48 crop years and the world prices for wheat in the 1946-47 and 1947-48 crop years.
It will be noted that the price for the 1948 crop was to be determined before December 31, 1947, and the price for the 1949 crop before December 31, 1948. In other words, the prices were to be determined seven months ahead of the beginning of the relevant crop year. Our two governments met ini the autumn of 1947 and determined upon a price of $2 per bushel for the 1948-49 crop year. Again in December, 1948, we met and determined upon a price of $2 per bushel for the 1949-50 crop year. If we knew then what we know now about world wheat supply and demand in the months that lay ahead, we might have been able to negotiate a higher price. In the circumstances then prevailing, $2 plus five to six cents carrying charges looked like a good price for 140 million bushels of wheat, and I think it was a good

Canadian Wheat Board Act price at which to sell such substantial quantities of wheat, particularly as the United Kingdom at that time anticipated that the international wheat agreement price would be $1.70 per bushel and that wheat could be purchased from countries other than Canada for the international wheat agreement price.
In January, 1949, it was agreed that final settlement under the have regard to clause would not be made at that time, but would be made before July 31, 1950. I went to London in May, 1950, for discussions having to do with marketing the 1950 crop. While there I discussed the wheat agreement, at the request of the United Kingdom. I reported thereon to the cabinet and to this house following my return. I had no authority, or indeed no reason to conclude any agreement with the British government. All I could do, and all I did do, was to report the position taken by the British government.
In brief, the British government stated positively that they had discharged their obligations under the agreement. They pointed out what I have pointed out in this statement, namely that there were risks on both sides in entering into an agreement for four years ahead covering such large quantities of grain.
That was an understandable attitude and, while I might have wished that the British government could have seen the advantage to them of making some further payments to Canadian wheat growers, I could not conscientiously say that they were in default under the agreement. I so reported to the cabinet, to this house and to the western wheat producers.
My own words in Hansard on June 5 of last year, though uttered on the spur of the moment and in the heat of debate, put the position as I have just stated it and I have no desire to alter them in any way.
On November 13, 1950, I gave a speech in Regina to the Saskatchewan wheat pool during which I dealt with the same point and perhaps with greater decision. I quote from my remarks at that time:
Now I personally went to London in May of this year for these final discussions. I found the attitude of the British government to be an understandable one. British authorities felt that they had taken sufficient forward risks during the life of the contract in guaranteeing us a market and they considered they had discharged their obligations under the "have regard" clause.
Quite apart from this issue, however, but out of respect for the way in which Canada and the United Kingdom had worked together in each other's interest in these post-war years, the United Kingdom undertook to purchase from Canada in the 1950-51 crop year-
That is the current year.
-its full requirement for North American wheat, provided price and quality to be not less favourable


than that obtainable from other North American sources. Probable United Kingdom requirement was estimated to be from 100 to 120 million bushels of wheat and flour on international wheat agreement terms. This undertaking was given with the knowledge that there would be little if any E.C.A. aid on purchases in Canada, and I have no doubt that the eminently fair way with which Canada has dealt with the United Kingdom under the contract these past four years had much to do with their giving us a forward assurance of a market for the present crop year, even though E.C.A. finance is available for any wheat or flour purchased in the United States.
As I have said, the British government has discharged its legal obligations under the agreement and is not in default. Subsequently, however, the Canadian government considered it advisable to inform the United Kingdom government of the views of certain producers' groups to the effect that sufficient account had not been taken in the final settlement of the so-called have regard to clause.
Accordingly, the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) mentioned the matter to Mr. Attlee when he was on a visit to Canada at the end of last year and again the Prime Minister had discussions in London in January. It was never suggested to the British government at any time that they were in legal default under the agreement. It was pointed out, however, that the existence of dissatisfaction among wheat producers in Canada about the results of the agreement could have unfortunate consequence for future trade relationships between our two countries and that the British government might wish to reconsider their earlier decision. My colleague, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), made similar representations a few weeks ago. As the house knows, however, the British government did not see fit to make any further payments.
That was a perfectly legal and proper decision for them to make under the agreement. The Canadian government, while recognizing that the legal obligations of the British government under the agreement had been fulfilled, took a different view of the over-all results and decided to pay into the five year pool the $65 million that remained under the United Kingdom loan act.
Personally, I think it was a mistake that there should have been included in the agreement such a loosely-worded have regard to clause. It has been a source of much misunderstanding in both the United Kingdom and Canada. I think the British government itself is partly to blame for the misunderstanding, for the speech by Mr. Strachey in Winnipeg undoubtedly led many producers to believe that the United Kingdom would act on a more generous interpretation.

Nevertheless, the agreement without that clause was by no means one-sided. It produced substantial benefits for Canadian producers as well as British consumers. It resulted in the highest average price for wheat ever realized by western wheat growers over a five-year period. But the have regard to clause was included, at the suggestion, as I recall it, of the United Kingdom government. Such a clause is not capable of precise meaning. The United Kingdom government took one view of it, which from their point of view was understandable. Our producers took another attitude which was equally understandable. Nevertheless, a clause in an agreement that is not subject to legal interpretation must inevitably be interpreted by the party that must do the paying. The other party may not agree, but he has no option but to accept.
That, hon. members of the House of Commons, is my view of the United Kingdom-Canada wheat agreement. I believe it was a good agreement. I believe it has been greatly to the advantage of the Canadian producers that that agreement was made. I cannot believe that we would have been able to deal with all the hazards involved in the marketing of those five crops without the British wheat agreement. I presume that we shall continue to have arguments as to the losses under the agreement. I do not know just from what point of view losses can be reckoned. People talk about the domestic price in the United States and they talk about the class 2 price of Canadian wheat. The domestic price of wheat in the United States at this moment is, I believe, about $2.42 a bushel. The price of class 2 Canadian wheat is probably about $2.18 a bushel. The international price of wheat today is probably about $1.87 a bushel. One can say that we can start right away to figure losses based on the fact that we are selling on the international wheat price. I do not know of any foreign markets to which the United States is sending its wheat and getting payment of the domestic price in cash. I think they are still operating largely under Marshall plan financing. Canada has posted a price of $2.18. They might as well make it $2.75 for all the effect it would have, because we have not sufficient milling wheat this year to fill our international wheat agreement, and therefore we are not in the market with any sizeable quantity of class 2 wheat. That is the position today. The position was similar in past years when there was a domestic price in the United States and a class 2 price in Canada. They were prices at which marginal quantities of wheat could be sold by both countries. It was not the price at which the bulk of the export wheat of the United States
Canadian Wheat Board Act was marketed. It was marketed under ECA funds and as a gift. It was not the price at which any very substantial quantities of Canadian wheat were marketed. But nevertheless it is very misleading and very fictitious to accept either the domestic price in the United States, the Chicago price or class 2 wheat price as representing the world price. They were not the same, and none of them represented anything more than the price which its name implies.
I might point out that in the years 1934 to 1938 which are more or less typical of marketing in pre-war years, our percentage of the British market was 52-5 per cent. In the year 1947 our part of the British market was 82-5 per cent. Of the crop grown in 1948 our wheat took 72-9 per cent of the British market, and for the year 1949 our wheat held 82-3 per cent of the British market. This year we would have had practically the entire British market had we been able to fill it. Unfortunately the frost damage in western Canada has made it impossible for us to fill even our quota under the international wheat agreement, as far as Britain is concerned; but they are taking anything we can offer them in the way of milling wheat.
It is well to keep in mind that our second market in the pre-war days was the Netherlands; and I may tell hon. gentlemen that we have hardly sold a bushel of wheat to the Netherlands since the war ended. Our next biggest market was Belgium. Belgium has supported our wheat, has bought sizeable quantities in the post-war years, for the reason that their supply of United States dollars was somewhat better than other countries. Italy was a great market. We are just now getting back into the Italian market in something like a substantial way, but there are other markets, which we have lost entirely for the reason that they were quite happy to buy wheat from the United States with ECA funds.
If anyone can view the position of Canada as a result of the four year agreement and say that it was a bad agreement, and quibble about whether we lost money under it or made money under it, that is their privilege; but I say that I am very happy the agreement was made. I am happy the way it has worked out, and I deplore the suggestion that the British government has not played fair with the Canadian people.

I think that every hon. member in this house will welcome the statement that has been made tonight by the Minister of Trade

Canadian Wheat Board Act and Commerce (Mr. Howe). My regret is that this statement was not made when this debate was first initiated. Had it been, a very great deal of the ill feeling that has been engendered, as I have very good reason to know, in western Canada, would not have been engendered. Local newspapers are coming in to Ottawa at the present time -I see my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle over there, one from his constituency, for example-with articles written by government supporters in this house denouncing the British government for breaking the agreement, for doing just exactly what the Minister of Trade and Commerce says was not done. And I am happy indeed tonight to think that the Minister of Trade and Commerce has been able to come before the house and make the statements that he has made.
I want to say to him that when this agreement was initiated, when it was before the house, we supported it. We believed, as the minister has said tonight, that it would give the western farmer some stability in his price. We believed that it was an excellent idea to try to get as large a share as we could for a period of years of the British market. We did say that if-as on August 15, 1946, it was quite evident it was going to do-inflation developed in this country and the cost of production rose, then at the end of the agreement a compensatory adjustment should be made, and that compensatory adjustment should come out of the federal treasury of Canada; that we could not go back to the British government at the end of the time and say: The costs of production in Canada have risen; the agreement was not as advantageous as we expected it to be, and therefore we expect you to pay something more than you have paid.
I remember very distinctly making that statement, and reiterating it; for I looked it up the day before yesterday in the debates on that occasion. I reiterated that opinion and that suggestion three or four times during the course of my speech on behalf of the members with whom I am associated, and suggested that if that occurred a compensatory adjustment should be made. That is what our amendment seeks now.
I did so on these grounds, that if the cost of production rose this government, having the control of the economy, would be responsible for making that compensatory adjustment. My hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) will recollect that he rose in his place that evening and pointed out to me and to the house that just as $200 million had been appropriated a few months before for the support of agricultural

prices other than wheat, a similar appropriation could be made if necessary for the wheat producers.
Since that date the costs of production of the eight principal products entering into the production of a bushel of wheat have risen from 128 points on August 1, 1946, to 194-2 points on August 1, 1950. That is the reason why in western Canada there was an agitation last fall, when the crop was frozen in the summer, when other conditions intervened, for a further payment than that which might have come from the agreement.
I wanted to make that clear because that was our position then. It is our position today.
We have never argued on the basis of what the price of wheat was to Great Britain, what the price of class 2 wheat was elsewhere, and made a comparison with the United States markets. We have pointed out that the cheap loaf enjoyed by the Canadian people during the war years was subsidized, not by the government of Canada, not by all the Canadian people, but by the prairie farmers who grew No. 1 wheat.
I listened to the Minister of Agriculture the other evening when he suggested that the amount was not as high as some people were saying, but that it probably was in the neighbourhood of $48 million; and it is on these two count? that we have suggested, and I still suggest to the government of Canada, that it was its obligation to make any further compensatory adjustments that the producers of western Canada were entitled to. And over the past few days, over the past week, I have asked a number of questions of the Minister of Agriculture. I must say that in all my experience in the house, extending over fifteen years, I have never seen a more reprehensible exhibition than the answers to those questions. I want to say this, as I said to some of my colleagues this morning, that the Minister of Trade and Commerce has come out of this well, and that nowhere in those questions and answers could I find anything other than he has admitted tonight. But when the Minister oi Agriculture was dealing with some of those matters I felt the house was being misled and was in danger of being deceived-and 1 say that is true of the country and true oi the western producers.
When the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent came in this afternoon he made a statemen to the house. I have not a copy of it, bu some of my colleagues took notes of it, an< I took a few notes. The result is that, puttini these notes together, I understood him to sa; exactly what the Minister of Trade and Com merce said tonight, that when he was ii

London he discussed this matter with the United Kingdom authorities, and that the United Kingdom took the position that all the obligations had been fulfilled on their part under this contract.
I recollect that when I asked the minister, earlier in the course of the debate, if he had agreed in London, the answer was no; if he had brought back a memorandum-and I might say to the house that when I was asking about bringing back a memorandum I was guessing: I had no knowledge of such a thing existing. I was just probing to find out. The minister said Yes, that he did, and that what was done with that memorandum was done in Ottawa. And from the Prime Minister's statement this afternoon that is made abundantly clear.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce said tonight, as he said before, as I understood the Prime Minister to say, that he said to the government in Great Britain that he had no authority to make an agreement, but that he would have to report the matter here and that whatever settlement was made would have to be made by the government in Ottawa.
And I have noticed!, too, from the questions and answers in this debate, that when the proposal-for such it was-made by the authorities in Great Britain to the government of Canada, through the Minister of Trade and Commerce, was approved by the cabinet, according to the Minister of Agriculture-and I believe the Minister of Trade and Commerce-it was approved unanimously. The Prime Minister this afternoon, if I am not mistaken, said that after the discussion the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who was the proper minister to do so, advised the Chancellor of the Exchequer- and I wrote down these words-that the Canadian government "was in accord with the conclusions"-and the Prime Minister nods his head-contained in what I understood to be the official document or official minute of the meeting held by the Minister of Trade and Commerce and representatives of the United; Kingdom in May of 1950.
If my understanding of what the Prime Minister said is correct-and I think it is, because the Minister of Trade and Commerce has confirmed it-the matter was settled very definitely and unanimously in Ottawa and the government of the United' Kingdom was so informed.

Prior to our entering confederation with Canada the British government arranged the convertibility of sterling. The bulk of our trade in salt fish was done in European markets, and as you know Great Britain is banker for the European countries. If Portugal bought fish, Britain would arrange that we in Newfoundland got dollars in return. That arrangement was continued until the first year after confederation. Now we owe Great Britain some $63 million, and that debt was assumed! by
i

Canada on confederation. The present situation is that the dominion owes the British government, on Newfoundland's account, some $63 million, but Britain contends that money is repayable not in sterling but in dollars. Now I am told that this year Britain is not prepared to undertake the conversion of this sterling. Britain says, "If you are going to pay back this money you cannot pay it back in sterling; you must pay it back in dollars." What I am afraid of, and I hope I am not blaming the minister unduly, is that all this ill will that has been stirred up in Britain over this wheat deal will gum up the works in relation to our sale of codfish. That is a very serious matter. You talk about having trouble in connection with wheat. If you get the Newfoundland fisherman in trouble with his codfish you will really be in for it.
I have made my point as well as I can. We had1 a clear statement this evening; and like the leader of the C.C.F. party (Mr. Coldwell) I think it is nice to learn that Britain is not being blamed for what happened under this wheat contract. The people of Britain have enough to put up with without being blamed in a matter of this nature. After five years of so-called peace Britons generally are putting up with an austerity program which we in Canada could never even contemplate. To blame these people, and to stir up ill will as has been done over this British wheat contract, is the most ungracious thing that the eldest daughter of the British commonwealth could possibly do. I am happy to hear that statement made tonight by the Minister of Trade and Commerce even though it was at the expense of the Minister of Agriculture. I believe the Minister of Agriculture will recognize and admit that it was no fault of the British people, and whatever idea he may have had of convincing the Attlee government to pay this money, there was no particular reason why the British people should have been blamed1 in the manner in which they have in this country within the past few weeks. I believe most members in this house will agree with that.
To sum up, Mr. Speaker, because I believe there are other people who want to say something in this debate, I am in favour of paying this money, and more besides, provided always that the maritimes get the same deal when they need; it, and that Newfoundland gets the same deal when she needs it, and the Ontario farmers as well. I do not believe that money should be taken from the Canadian taxpayers to pay this $65 million unless we get that deal right across the board generally. Those are my sentiments. Where the money will come from, to pay it, is another matter.

The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), western Liberal farmers, Canadian farmers in general, all parties made some interesting comments and produced interesting figures. It is a market we badly need.
There is one group of people in Canada, and that is the great mass of taxpayers, who must be wondering how much longer this government, when it enters a deal, will use every means in its power to try to get more money for the people it represents, although the government is firmly convinced it is not entitled' to it according to the statement by the Minister of Trade and Commerce tonight. Mr. Speaker, I had intended to speak tonight in such a way as I thought would establish the truth which the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) so well expressed before -this house. I have viewed with the

deepest regret the development of a campaign to smear Great Britain. That campaign has involved several of the responsible members of this house, as can easily be shown by quotations from their remarks in one place or another, and in their ridings. I was intending to answer the kind of thing which they were endeavouring to establish. As the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) has indicated, matters have in some places got to fever heat in this country. People have almost reached the point where they will hardly discuss Britain -at all; and all that has occurred with no justification at all, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce has so well put it. But since the Minister of Trade and Commerce has relieved me of that burden, I shall devote myself to certain other matters which I believe it would be well to probe into.
To my way of thinking, as a result of the discussions we have had thus far, four obvious conclusions have been established. The first is that the Canadian wheat growers ought to receive a final payment of 25 cents a bushel; not less and probably a good deal more, as the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) well developed the other day in his speech. The second conclusion is that for paying -any part of this 25 -cents a bushel Britain appears to have no kind or degree of obligation, either legal or moral. I can now say that without any question at all, since the Minister of Trade and Commerce has spoken. The third conclusion is that the Canadian government ought to pay that 25 cents a bushel. The fourth conclusion I am afraid has to be this-and I hope I shall not use words that are too harsh or too strong in their implication in saying what I feel I must say: Some persons connected with the Liberal Canadian government, it appears, have deliberately contrived to -cast upon Britain blame and odium which justly should rest upon a certain group of members deep in the Liberal party itself.
This general scheme was well set forth and well developed by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) the other day in his speech which is recorded at pages 1093 to 1098 of 1951 Hansard. It looks as though someone had put these men up to this thing and that each had said his little piece, made his little bow and gone out. I believe that every hon. member of this house and every person in this country will be positively astounded that a thing like this could have occurred. It is a matter which is utterly reprehensible. Whoever organized that thing has done something that no man with responsibility should ever contemplate for a minute. In times like these, when the enemy is right at our door, and when every person is straining to the limit, it is astounding that anyone should start an outrageous thing like this for the purpose of sowing discord and unhappiness in the Dominion of Canada and cause those feelings to be reflected by the British over on the other side of the water; it is something that just passes human comprehension that a thing of that sort could have been done.
The Liberal strategy to blame Britain-and it must have been the Liberal strategy of somebody-was, to put the matter bluntly, nothing but a dastardly political device for dishonouring Canadian commitments both to Canada's wheat growers and to the British. Hon. members who participated in this pernicious program of propaganda calculated to delude the Canadian people into doubting Britain's good' faith as to her honouring the Canadian wheat agreement of 1946 to 1950- those men have done Britain and Canada a serious disservice. I think that mere justice demands that words as harsh as these should be used.
May I take a moment to sum up each of the four conclusions that I have come to. The first one was that Canadian farmers ought to receive a final payment of 25 cents a bushel at least on their wheat. I know that the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Ferguson) was expressing very honourably and straightforwardly the point of view of a large number of people in the Dominion of Canada. To him it looks as though it is proposed to take from the Canadian people's pockets a vast sum of money and give that money outright to one section of the Canadian people. To him that looks to be completely unsound in every way.
I shall not have time to deal with this matter adequately tonight. I shall speak as long as I have an opportunity to and then I shall go on the next time this debate comes up; because, after all, it is a problem with which the Canadian people will have to come to grips.

Here was a great body of producers, Canadian producers, the farmers of western Canada. They were producing a commodity absolutely essential in the conduct of the war. We have manufacturers in Canada who were asked at the beginning of world war II whether they would produce guns, tanks, aeroplanes, bullets and other munitions of war. They said: We will not produce one single unit until you guarantee us costs of production plus a certain percentage. Now, I think no one in the House of Commons, unless it may be some of my C.C.F. friends, will question the soundness of their position. I surely do not.
If their position was sound as producers of the munitions of war, will anyone tell me that the position of the western farmer is not equally sound if he says:	I want to be
guaranteed the cost of production plus a just profit.
The question at issue is this. Have the western farmers in the production of their wheat been guaranteed the cost of production plus a just profit?
